  Deep learning models for diagnostic and prognostic pathology often require
analysis of whole slide images (WSIs) at the level of hundreds of microns.
Extracting and classifying regions of interest (ROIs) of various sizes is a
critical step in this process. A major obstacle in developing and testing such
deep learning models is the problem of data scale, i.e., the volume of the
input data relative to the capacity to process it. A major advantage of
federated learning (FL) is its ability to train deep learning models on
datasets that are partitioned over numerous nodes, without the need to
collect the data at a centralized location. Here, we investigate the use of
SLIC superpixels to enable analysis of WSIs using a patch size that is
optimally scaled to the underlying histology. Also, we evaluate the performance
of FL in developing deep learning models for analysis of WSIs. A classification
application was considered as the example use case, on quantifying the
distribution of tumor infiltrating lymphocytes. A classification model was
trained using 200*200 square micron patches extracted from the WSIs. Our results
show that the model trained with the federated training approach achieved
significant performance gains, both quantitatively and qualitatively, likely
due to the ability to analyze SLIC superpixels of size patches that are
optimally scaled to the underlying histology.

detector designs for the future International
Linear Collider (ILC) in which to study physics processes at high energy. SiD
is a compact detector with excellent tracking and identification of jets and
missing energy, and excellent capability to identify high energy photons and
pairs of particles. SiD is optimised for precision Higgs and other measurements
in addition to searches for beyond Standard Model processes. SiD software
development starts early in the SiD R\&D program and is now underway in
collaboration with other ILC detector groups. The software architecture is
developed with RePrository as the central component of the SiD software
infrastructure. This talk presents the current status of the SiD software
development and focuses on the tracking software development within SiD.
  In this contribution we report on the performance of the two tracking
algorithms, the Grid Based Tracking (GBT) and the Standar Template Approach (STA),run so far in the SiD simulation framework, called SiDCC. We study the
performance of the tracking for the ILC momentum range from 20 to 100 GeV. The
study shows that both tracking algorithms have similar performance. The hit
efficiency is around 97\% for the track curvature larger than 1~GeV/c and the
direction resolution better than 3~mrad for all the momenta. We also report on
the proper operation of the optical track clubs used in the test beam program
and the performance of the track reconstruction in a real time environment.
Finally, the small effect of the beam background on the tracking is also shown.
In general the performance of the tracking is in line with the SiD design
requirements.
  Finally, it is worth to mention that the SiDCC framework is now fully
integrated with other ILC detector software frameworks, including the ILD
software. This is an important step towards the simulation of an ILC detector.
In fact, for the benefit of all ILC detector designers, we are working towards
the integration of all detector software into a common framework, called
"Integration Framework". SiDCC is an integral part of it.

linearization theorem for smooth vector fields which admit a complete set of
first integrals near a nondegenerate singular point. The main tools used in the
proof of this theorem are the formal orbital linearization theorem for formal
integrable vector fields, the blowing-up method, and the Sternberg-Chen

  From the point of view of formal theory of singularities, the formal
orbital linearization theorem for formal integrable vector fields was classical
(see [20, Chapter 4]), and its proof can be found in many sources (see e.g. [6,
11, 16, 20]). The new part in the proof of the smooth orbital
linearization theorem is to get rid of formal singularities of vector fields.
This is done by blowing up the singularities in suitable spaces of wave fronts
of functions and vectors. Because the blowing-up procedure changes the
singularities of functions and vectors but not their formal integrability, the
formal orbital linearization theorem still applies. The final step in the proof
of the smooth orbital linearization theorem is to get rid of the local
hyperbolicity assumption. This is done by reducing the general case to the
hyperbolic one using a result of Sternberg and Chen (see [21]).

integrability of a vector field, of a formal/sMOOTH singularities of a vector
field, of a formal/sMOOTH hyperbolic vector field. In Section 2 we prepare the
ground for the blowing-up procedure by introducing a space of wave fronts of
functions and a norm on this space. We also prove a genericity lemma for
functions and vectors, we introduce a space of hyperbolic vectors equipped with
a norm, and we prove the formal orbital linearization theorem for formal
integrable vector fields. In Section 3 we blow up the singularities of the
integrable vector field from Section 2, and thus we get a sequence of
formally-equivalent hyperbolic vector fields. In Section 4 we get rid of the
local hyperbolicity assumption by using a result of Sternberg and Chen. In
Section 5 we take away the blow-ups made in Section 3.

convolutional neural network (CNN) has received considerable attention.
Depending on whether intermediate cues are used, the relevant literature can be
roughly divided into two broad categories: direct methods and two stage
pipelines. For the latter, intermediate cues, such as 3D object coordinates,
semantic keypoints, or virtual control points instead of pose parameters are
regressed by CNN in the first stage. Object pose can then be solved by
correspondence constraints constructed with these intermediate cues. In this
paper, we focus on the postprocessing of a two-stage pipeline and propose to
combine two learning concepts for estimating object pose under challenging
scenes: projection grouping on one side, and correspondence learning on the
other. We firstly employ a local patch based method to predict projection
heatmaps which denote the confidence distribution of projection of 3D bounding
box's corners. A projection grouping module is then proposed to remove
redundant local maxima from each layer of heatmaps. Instead of directly feeding
2D-3D correspondences to the perspective-n-point (PnP) algorithm, multiple
correspondence hypotheses are sampled from local maxima and its corresponding
neighborhood and ranked by a correspondence-evaluation network. Finally,
correspondences with higher confidence are selected to determine object pose.
Extensive experiments on three public datasets demonstrate that the proposed
framework achieves better performance than several state-of-the-art methods.
Moreover, our framework attaches only two small CNNs to perform pose estimation
and thus is scalable to deal with object categories for which large-scale
3D-annotated datasets are difficult to collect.

lidar point cloud as input, and then refine the translation with a secondary
network incorporating corresponding individual inputs. We further propose a
novel matching strategy to associate 2D image features with 3D lidar points
and vice versa, for fulfilling intermediate correspondence assumption of the
PnP algorithm. Experimental results on two public datasets indicate that the
proposed framework achieves superior performance against baselines and
state-of-the-art methods.

variant of eigenvector centrality
for multilayer networks with inter-layer constraints on node importance.
Specifically, we consider a multilayer network defined by multiple
edge-weighted, potentially directed, graphs over the same set of nodes with
each graph representing one layer of the network and no inter-layer edges. As
in the standard eigenvector centrality construction, the importance of each
node in a given layer is based on the weighted sum of the importance of
adjacent nodes in that same layer. Unlike standard eigenvector centrality, we
assume that the adjacency relationship and the importance of adjacent nodes may
be based on distinct layers. Importantly, this type of centrality constraint is
only partially supported by existing frameworks for multilayer eigenvector
centrality that use edges between nodes in different layers to capture
inter-layer dependencies. For our model, constrained, layer-specific
eigenvector centrality values are defined by a system of independent eigenvalue
problems and dependent pseudo-eigenvalue problems, whose solution can be
efficiently realized using an existing algorithm. Our approach and method are
validated by a careful analysis and several numerical examples.
  We demonstrate that our approach can capture inter-layer dependencies that
existing multilayer eigenvector centrality methods cannot capture and provide
accurate rankings of node importance in a network for a variety of networks and
mock networks. Our approach can also help to identify layers in a real network
that contribute most to the overall centrality of each node and thus to its
effective connectivity within the network.
  In addition, we consider a novel procedure to obtain a measure of independence
between the centrality of a node in different layers (i.e., the layer-specific
eigenvector centrality) and the network's overall eigenvector centrality and
show how it can be used to define a layer-specific degree of node centrality.
Finally, we show that this measure of independence can also be used to define a
novel measure of node transitivity across layers.
  In conclusion, our procedure can be used to define a family of multilayer
eigenvector centrality measures, each with a different set of assumptions about
node importance and/or adjacency relationships across layers. These measures can
be used to study a network from different perspectives and can provide
independent information about node transitivity and the importance of each
layer in the definition of node centrality.

metries should be absent in
quantum gravity. By investigating large classes of Type IIB four-dimensional
$\mathcal{N}=2$ effective field theories, we enlist the potential generalized
global symmetries that could be present and explore how they are avoided.
Crucial ingredients that arise in such effective field theories are generalized
$\theta$-terms. These introduce non-linear couplings between axion fields and
topological terms quadratic in the gauge field strengths which break a large
subset of the global symmetries. Additional residual global symmetries may
further be broken by assuming the existence of some charged states. However, we
illustrate that the presence of generalized $\theta$-terms leads to a
generalized Witten effect, which implies that the spectrum of charged states is
constituted by an infinitely populated lattice. We further show that such a
lattice is generated by the action of the monodromy transformation that
characterizes the moduli space boundary near which the effective theory is
defined.
  Finally, we stress that the absence of global symmetries may be a general
feature of effective field theories living on branches of moduli space that are
lifted in string theory. The treatment presented here is purely effective and
provides a motivation for further investigation of four-dimensional $\mathcal{N}=1$
effective field theories, which are the lowest effective theories that typically
live on branches of the moduli space controlled by Calabi-Yau geometries.
Interestingly, the absence of global symmetries in Type IIB theory would also
implies the non-existence of a real Klebsch-Gordon invariant, which is a
topological term that appears in $\mathcal{N}=1$ effective field theories as a
generalized $\theta$-term.

device as other untrusted and potentially malicious programs. This requires
users to trust hardware and system software to correctly sandbox malicious
programs, trust that is often misplaced.
  Our goal is to minimize the number and complexity of hardware and software
components that a smartphone owner needs to trust to withstand adversarial
inputs. We present a multi-domain hardware design composed of
statically-partitioned, physically-isolated trust domains. We introduce a few
simple, formally-verified hardware components to enable a program to gain
provably exclusive and simultaneous access to both computation and I/O on a
temporary basis. To manage this hardware, we present OctopOS, an OS composed of
mutually distrustful subsystems.
  We present a prototype of this machine (hardware and OS) on a CPU-FPGA board
and show that it incurs a small hardware cost compared to modern SoCs. For
security-critical programs, we show that this machine significantly reduces the
required trust compared to mainstream TEEs while achieving decent performance.
For normal programs, performance is similar to a legacy machine.
  We believe that the approach of composing a program's trust domains dynamically
is generalizable to other hardware designs, which could make this style of
security widely available.

considered in prior works. Our first result shows that no algorithm can find a

robustness property if the reward corruption is bounded, and can find an

Gradient (FPG) algorithm that can tolerate even unbounded reward corruption and
can find an $O(\epsilon^{1/4})$-optimal policy. We emphasize that FPG is the
first that can achieve a meaningful learning guarantee when a constant fraction
of episodes are corrupted. Complimentary to the theoretical results, we show
that a neural implementation of FPG achieves strong robust learning performance
on the MuJoCo continuous control benchmarks.
  Our theory answer the following questions: (1) Can reinforcement learning
algorithms be attacked by adapting the transition and reward functions within
an episode?, (2) How much error can be introduced while still maintaining
learning ability?, and (3) How do different attack models relate to standard
measurements of statistical learning error? Such a study is important because
attack and learning are complementary and often used as tools to evaluate the
robustness of learning algorithms, but have not been systematically analyzed.
We show that the answer to (1) is negatively -- all algorithms will converge to
a suboptimal policy if the transition and reward are adaptively corrupted within
an episode. Next we define the \textit{adaptive error} measurement and show in

$O(\epsilon)$. We show that the answer to (3) depends on the measurement of
adaptive error, and discuss the relationship between adaptive error and

semiconductor quantum dot pumped by a driving laser, and coupled to an acoustic
cavity. This kind of systems has proven to yield interesting multi-phonon
phenomena, but the description of the quantum dot has been limited to a
two-level system. This limitation restrains the complexity that a true
semiconductor quantum dot can offer. Instead, in this work we consider a model
where the quantum dot can have both bright and dark excitons, the latter being
particularly useful due to their lower decoherence rates, because they do not
present spontaneous photon emission. In this setup, we demonstrate that by
fine-tuning the driving laser frequency, one is able to realise giant Rabi
oscillations between the vacuum state and a dark exciton state with $N$-phonon
bundles. From this, we highlight two outstanding features: first, we are able
to create dark states excitations in the quantum dot without the usual external
magnetic field needed to do so; and second, in a dissipative scenario where the
acoustic cavity and the quantum dot present dissipation, we are able to
observable giant Rabi oscillations for a very large number of phonons $N$.
Specifically, we are able to create oscillations between the vacuum state and
dark exciton states with $N=4$ when the dissipation in the system is 80%\ of
its maximum possible value. This is an unusually large value of $N$ for which
one is able to observe such features, and it is an evidence of the particular
importance of the dark excitons states in this kind of system.

total decoherence rate of the system by roughly four order of magnitudes. This

addressing global challenges, such as climate change, sustainable energy, and
healthy living. The discovery of such compounds often starts with designing
the molecular structure of a compound with a desired chemical property. One of
the major methods for achieving this goal relies on expert chemists who have
extensive knowledge of chemical compounds and properties as well as computational
tools to propose, evaluate, and modify potential candidates. One of the major
drawbacks of this method is that it relies on the expertise and time of human
chemists. To address this limitation, researchers have proposed algorithms that
generate candidates and evaluate them using predictive functions. One such
algorithms is the one proposed in [1] that designs the molecular structure of a
chemical compound with a desired chemical property using both artificial
neural networks and mixed integer linear programming. In this paper, we design a
new method for inferring a polymer based on the framework of [1]. For this, we
introduce a new way of representing a polymer as a form of monomer and define
new descriptors that feature the structure of polymers. We also use linear
regression as a building block of constructing a prediction function in the
framework. The results of our computational experiments reveal a set of chemical
properties on polymers for which a prediction function constructed with linear
regression performs well. We also observe that the proposed method can infer
polymers with up to 50 non-hydrogen atoms in a monomer form.

to be very challenging. This is due to the low contrast between the tumor and
adjacent tissues, the anatomical variation of the esophagus, as well as the
occasional presence of foreign bodies (e.g. feeding tubes). Physicians
therefore usually exploit additional knowledge such as endoscopic findings,
clinical history, additional imaging modalities like PET scans. Achieving his
additional information is time-consuming, while the results are error-prone and
might lead to non-deterministic results. In this paper we aim to reduce the
need for these additional investigations by improving the accuracy of
esophageal tumor segmentation on CT data via a novel approach that uses
stacked progressive density networks (SPD-Net) to accurately segment the
esophagus and the tumor for better input for the next step. We evaluate our
method on two public datasets: the CLovDsec dataset and the SASHIMON dataset,
obtained from the SASHIMON database. Our evaluation shows that the proposed
method outperforms other state-of-the-art methods, both quantitatively and
visually.

superior results compared to established methods, see Table 1 and Figure 1.

see Figure 2, (iii) SPD-Net adapts to the presence of foreign bodies see Figure
3, (iv) SPD-Net adapts to non-uniform image characteristics see Figure 4.
Therefore, we conclude that SPD-Net is suitable for esophageal tumor delineation
from CT data, which can be used as a standalone segmentation task or as an
input for subsequent analysis, e.g. lesion volume measurement or texture
extraction.

  Multilingualism refers to the high degree of proficiency in two or more
languages in the written and oral communication modes. It often results in
language mixing, when a multilingual speaker switches between multiple languages
in a single utterance of a text or speech. Crisis management, healthcare,
political campaigning, fake news, and hate speech are some of the applications
for social good that involve languages of the internet. However, the performance
of the applications is degraded by the language mixing in real world data.
Therefore, the NLP research community must address the problems like named
entity recognition, sentiment analysis, machine translation, hate speech
detection, and text classification for language of the internet. In this paper,
we discuss the state of the art research, limitations, and foreseeable pitfalls
in multilingual text processing for the above applications. We also propose
data, models, and tools that can significantly advance the current research in
multilingual NLP applications for the societal good. As a representative example,
we consider English-Hindi code-mixing but draw similar inferences for other
language pairs.

determination of the translation direction based on them. The latter model
generates VM to EM or EM to VM translation given the code-mixed utterance in VM.

  Few-shot learning (FSL)  is a learning paradigm to classify new categories

methods, which represents classes with the mean feature of support samples.
Here, we treat the prototype  as a low-dimensional manifold and the
corresponding operator can be seen as a transformation that maps the support
feature to the prototype. To enhance the representativeness of prototypes,
instead of merely averaging support features, we propose to use the operator to
augment prototypes. Specifically, we use the linear operator to achieve this
goal. Extensive experiments demonstrate its effectiveness. Notably, it

Representations for FSL (TADEM)  effectively generates such knowledge by
generating negative samples to enhance the distinguishability of prototypes.
Here, we propose to directly improve the representativeness of prototypes by
incorporating the combined feature of support samples with the help of neural
operators.

become essential, especially for larger scale analysis. Several attempts have

generalization of these methods on new data independent of those used for
learning is a difficult problem because of the biases inherent in MRI data.
This work aimed at evaluating the performances of the MRIQC pipeline on various
large-scale datasets (ABIDE, N = 1102 and CATI derived datasets, N = 9037) and
to further aggregate the results using two approaches (mean and resampling)
leading to summary scores per image. We first assessed the T1w, T2w, DWi, MOWix
and ROI intensity QC methods on synthetic images with gradually increasing
errors. We then applied two post-processing methods on the failure flags
generated by MRIQC: a rule-based and a learning-based method. We evaluated the
benefits of adding these methods after MRIQC. We finally compared the
performances of the different pipelines.
  Our results on synthetic images showed that the DWi QC method is robust to
increasing errors (up to 50%) while the MOWix and ROI intensity methods are
more sensitive. The T1w and T2w QC methods are the less robust ones. We also
highlighted that the aggregation methods lead to very similar results. We
further show that the scores obtained using the resampling method are strongly
right skewed, which is not the case for the mean method. We suggest using the
mean method for subject level scoring and the resampling method for image
quality ranking. Finally, we found that about 1.5% of the images score 2 or
higher, which means that they contain obvious artifacts. Using a quality score
allows to visualize the quality distribution of an image, to remove poor
images and to weight them in order to prevent biases in analysis.

pipeline that includes T1w, T2w, DWi, MOWix and ROI intensity QC methods. We
further suggest to use a rule-based method after the MRIQC pipeline in order to
remove images with obvious failures and to improve the robustness of the
pipeline.
  Finally, we provide a new open-source pipeline that includes MRIQC, a rule
based method and a learning based method for QC score aggregation.

detectors. We create a new context benchmark to evaluate detectors consisely

surprisingly well-studied and some methods are specialized to exploit context
perfectly for specific categories of images. We also reveal detectors which are
prone to erroneous use of context and perform significantly worse on our
benchmark. From experimental analysis, we propose a theory of context for
object detectors which leads to a context-based evaluation framework. Our
method is freely usable by the community to evaluate object detectors for a
variety of context sensitive tasks like pedestrian detection, co-localization

reason is the cost of integrating out the auxiliary variables, even if done
using approximate methods like JAGS MH updating within each loop or using

which are the counterparts of our optimal wideband waveforming strategy in [1].
The fair-throughput and the sum-throughput optimisation problems are
formulated. By exploiting the FP based alternating algorithm, we obtain the
optimal fair-throughput and sum-throughput for both the SISO-OFDM and
MISO-OFDM.
  In the fair-throughput optimisation, we devise the joint power loading and
precoding design. We fix the power loadings and then utilise the DP based
optimisation to obtain the optimal precoding vector. After that, we update the
power allocations by solving a convex problem with Inverse Inequality Constraints
(IICs) and a largest eigenvalue maximisation (LEM) form subject to general
economy of scale power constraints (GESPCs). We also propose a suboptimal but
efficiently solvable scheme by adding the sum power constraint (SPC) and the
minimum power constraint (MPC) in sequence. Both of the optimal and suboptimal
schemes are capable of being implemented via the DP and Jacobi iterative methods
respectively. Lastly, we devise a suboptimal fair-throughput design, which
exploys the fixed precoding matrix instead of the pointwise optimal design. This
suboptimal design is also capable of being implemented via the convex programme
CP1 with joint power loading and user selection, and the suboptimal power
allocation with a convex form subject to the GESPCs.
  In the sum-throughput optimisation, we propose the suboptimal sum-throughput
designs by utilising the fixed precoding matrix, the joint power loading and
user selection, and the suboptimal power allocation with a convex form,
respectively. All of the suboptimal designs are capable of removing the IPCs
and/or the SCs. We show that the best suboptimal design should remove the SPC
and the MPC to guarantee the largest possible number of the supported users.
  Simulations show that the suboptimal designs presented in this article are
capable of achieving a large portion of the optimal sum-throughput performance,
while providing a much faster convergence rate than the iterative scheme. It is
also shown that the joint power loading and user selection suboptimal design
can outperform the suboptimal power allocation design in terms of the sum
throughput.

the implementation, numerical tests and first results of a large suite of
cosmological simulations for three classes of MG models with conformal coupling
terms: the $f(R)$ gravity, symmetron and coupled quintessence models. Derived
from the parallel particle-mesh code GLAM, MG-GLAM incorporates an efficient
multigrid relaxation technique to solve the characteristic nonlinear partial
differential equations of these models. For $f(R)$ gravity, we have included
new variants to diversify the model behaviour, and we have tailored the
relaxation algorithms to these to maintain high computational efficiency. In a
companion paper, we describe versions of this code developed for derivative
coupling MG models, including the Vainshtein- and K-mouflage-type models.

and versatile. The code is highly optimised, with a tremendous speedup of a
factor of more than a hundred compared with earlier $N$-body codes, while still
giving accurate predictions of the matter power spectrum and dark matter halo
abundance. MG-GLAM is ideal for the generation of large numbers of MG
simulations that can be used in the construction of mock galaxy catalogues for
observational comparisons and cosmological structure formation studies.

these models, and it correctly reproduces the effects of the MG term on the
evolution and clustering of dark matter haloes. For example, halo masses are
known to be increased (decreased) in $f(R)$ gravity by up to a factor of almost
two for the highest (lowest) halo masses that form in a given volume. MG-haloes

us to easily investigate these effects in a variety of different simulation
designs, and it is a vital tool for the interpretation of $f(R)$ gravity
simulations. When modelling realistic galaxy formation with MG-GLAM, as in the
construction of mock galaxy catalogues, it is essential to include the effect of
the MG term on the internal structure and dynamics of dark matter haloes.

intended to be easy to use, and a "quick start" guide is included in the

different and richer than that of repulsively-bound on-site clusters in gases
without inter-site interactions. Whereas on-site pairs move in the same way as
individual particles, nearest-neighbor dimers perform an interacting quantum
walk with an effective mass and dispersion different from those of individual
particles. This is demonstrated both analytically, using a dimerization
approach valid for small binding energies, and numerically in the context of
the extended-Hubbard and XXZ models. Furthermore, we show that dimer quantum
walk in the XXZ model leads to robust, stable, and symmetric propagation of
boundonelonger clusters (trimers). This is unusual in repulsive zero-range
processes, where three-body bound states are generally not more stable than
two-body ones. The dynamics of these trimers is also different from that of
freely-interacting particles. The phenomenon of the dimer walk is generic and
should be observable in various systems of ultracold gases.

to each other, forming links of length 3. Furthermore, pairs of these links
bind into staircases of length 5. This rich structure of bound clusters may
lead to interesting phenomena, such as macroscopic quantum wave functions.
Lastly, we discuss how the dynamics of these clusters can be observed in
experiments.

the MI and the LMI phases. Our work may lead to new insights into strongly

annotations for driving behaviors can be derived from it. We argue that once

to resolve the $g-2$ anomaly is found to be insensitive to the specific EFT

can be transformed into a trivial unknot diagram by a series of unknotting
operations plus some Reidemeister moves. Unknotting operations have significant
importance in knot theory; they are used to study the complexity of knots and
invariants of knots. Unknotting operations are also important in biology,
chemistry, and physics to study the sophisticated entanglements of strings,
organic compounds, and DNA. In this paper, we introduced a new unknotting
operation called the diagonal move for classical and welded knots. We show that
the crossing change, Delta-move, Sharp-move, Gamma-move, n-gon move, pass move,
and 4-move can be realized by a sequence of diagonal moves. We also define the
distance induced by the diagonal move and study its properties.

their diagonal move complexes. By this, we give a new inequality on the diagonal
move distance. We also give a lower bound on the crossing change distance with
respect to the diagonal move distance.
  For the diagonal move distance on classical knots, we give an upper bound and
show that it is at most 3 times the crossing change distance plus 4.

show that it is equivalent to the cutting move distance introduced by C. Adams,
M. Giannini, and O. Yilmaz.

knots. Similarly, the genus diagonal move distance gives a new inequality on the
genus of knots.

very often to solve their own problems. The most often matrix operation is the
multiplication. It may be time-consuming if the matrices to be multiplied are
large. For this reason, the parallel computer became a must to tackle this
problem. In this report, it is presented a comparison between sequential and
parallel approaches to computing the matrix multiplication using CUDA and
openMP. The results show the importance of parallelizing mainly when the
matrices are large.

arguably more suitable for joint model training between large enterprises.

real-world VFL frameworks. We design and implement practical revenge learning
attacks for a popular open-source VFL framework called Private AI Library (PAI)

normal user access can steal the logistic regression model's prediction
labels, and further obtain the sensitive labels (e.g., medical labels) of
users' private data. We also show the adversary can leak the decision function
of the learned model, i.e., breast cancer diagnosis, by predicting on different
images with and without tumor. Finally, we discuss the limitations of the
leaked information and propose remedies to mitigate potential privacy leaks in
PAI.

practical revenge learning attacks, i.e., label leakage attack (LLA) and decision
leakage attack (DLA), for PAI. (2) We evaluate the success of LLA and DLA in
extracting sensitive labels and decision functions of different learning models,

sequentiality-aware pretraining techniques that exploit the sequential

information, which is a common complaint from manual authors. To provide more
free and flexible temporal signals, we propose to generate descriptive captions
over instructional images and show that it effectively improves machines'
performance by > 11%.

that can be obtained with graphene. Here we propose a
graphene-Bernal-layer-copper compound GBLC as an interface material between
graphene and Bernal copper oxide with correlation parameters of the copper
layer: $U=3$eV, $J=0.7$eV. We show that many novel, interaction-induced
electronic and magnetic states appear in the GBLC model. Among them are:
anti-ferromagnetic Mott-Hubbard state with spin-polarized Dirac bands,
superconductivity induced by the pair-hopping process, a spin-charge separation
and a spin-polarized electron-hole symmetry. The magnetic and superconducting
phases in the GBLC model are also obtained when both $U$ and $J$ are present.
In this case, the many-body effects are controlled by the anisotropy of the
Coulomb interaction, $J/U\approx 0.233$ being close to the magic value $J/U=1$.
We conclude that the GBLC model represents a versatile interface system which
exhibits a wide range of interaction-induced physics.
  We also propose two GBLC-based devices: a spin-polarized Dirac arc detector
and a spin-charge separation switch.
  The spin-polarized Dirac arc detector can work as both spin filter and spin
detector. The spin-charge separation switch can be used either as a spin
switch (when only the spin-polarized Dirac arc is present) and as a charge
switch (when only the spin-charge separation is present).

charge to spin.

10^{13}$Hz$^{-1}$.

in a solid state system.

identify singularities of maximally mutable Laurent polynomials and their

Fano/Landau-Ginzburg correspondent. As in our previous work, the key ingredient
in the construction of the transform is the technique of analytic or
subanalytic cohomology classes. These classes carry information of the
local geometry of the Laurent polynomial and its modification to its
Fano/Landau-Ginzburg correspondent. The transform can be seen as a tool that
propagates this information from a maximally mutable Laurent polynomial to its

for the threefolds given by quaternions with norm 2 avoids the standard

the performance of Informed OCR or
iOCR. iOCR was developed with a spell correction algorithm to fix errors
introduced by conventional OCR for vote tabulation. The results found that the
iOCR system outperforms conventional OCR techniques.
  From a technical standpoint, iOCR represents a set of strategies for
improving the accuracy of optical character recognition of paper-based
documents through postprocessing with human language knowledge. iOCR was
developed as a spell correction algorithm to fix errors introduced by conventional
OCR techniques.
  The results found that the iOCR system outperforms conventional OCR techniques.
For example, iOCR corrected 57 out of 500 incorrect characters, while conventional
OCR techniques corrected only 7 out of 500 incorrect characters.
  iOCR is widely applicable to any document type with some level of pre-processing.
For example, iOCR was used to improve voting system verification and audit
processes. It was also found to outperform conventional OCR techniques for
voting system verification and audit processes.
  In conclusion, iOCR represents a system with the potential to improve
accuracy of paper document recognition beyond what is currently achievable with
conventional OCR techniques.
  Future iOCR development strategies are also discussed.

  Word Sense Disambiguation (WSD), a classical natural language processing
problem, is to identify the sense of a polysemous word in a specific context.
Over the past decades, numerous studies have been conducted on this problem and
different approaches have been proposed. Recently, deep-learning techniques
using BERT have achieved very promising results (Camacho-Callas et al., 2020;
Ji et al., 2020) and different methods have been proposed to integrate
structured knowledge to enhance performance (Yaghoubzadeh et al., 2020; QDY
et al., 2020b). Among them, using WordNet glosses is a promising approach.

relationships and glosses (Miller, 1995). Previous works have demonstrated its
effectiveness in improving WSD performance (Leaman et al., 2007; Guadalupe and
Strassel, 2007; QDY et al., 2020b). In this paper, we explore different data
augmentation techniques on context-gloss pairs to further improve WSD
performance.

to the publication of graphs and their associated statistics as well as machine
learning on graph-based data, including graph neural networks (GNNs). The
formulation of DP in the context of graph-structured data is difficult, as
individual data points are interconnected (often non-linearly or sparsely).
This connectivity complicates the computation of individual privacy loss in
differentially private learning. The problem is exacerbated by the fact that
even if the direct connection between two individuals is sparse, connections
may exist through a chain of connections, thus potentially compromising
privacy. The field of graph-based DP research is unique, as it offers
opportunities for interesting connections with other disciplines, e.g.,
algebraic topology and persistent homology. In this work, we refrain from
presenting a survey of the field of graph DP, and instead focus on discussing
the algorithms and theories applicable to graph analysis while ensuring the
data analysis respects DP. We aim to provide a unique perspective on graph DP
which ties together the discrete mathematics underlying graph theory with the
statistical science of DP.

new stochastic hydrodynamic method for the description of interacting Bose

fluctuations. Future works will investigate to what extent such a manipulation
can be used to alter the edge turbulence and the plasma-wall interactions in a

testing, the gold standard for evaluating test quality is mutation analysis,
assessing the ability of a test to detect synthetic bugs; if a set of tests
fails to detect such mutations, it will also fail to detect real bugs. Mutation
analysis subsumes various coverage measures and provides a large and diverse
set of faults that can be arbitrarily hard to trigger and detect, thus
preventing the problems of saturation and overfitting. Unfortunately, the cost
of traditional mutation analysis is exorbitant for fuzzing, as mutations need
independent evaluation.

majority of mutations. Unfortunately, most fuzzers, however, fail to improve
their coverage beyond what simple random testing provides. Interestingly,
comparing delimiters (e.g., timeout vs. seeding) and evaluation metrics (e.g.,
speed-up vs. coverage) matters when evaluating fuzzers. Finally, we show that
the evaluation of fuzzers is highly dependent on the target, and a deluded
evaluation on easy targets can lead to incorrect conclusions on harder targets.

$\lambda$-Lipschitz games in which every player's payoff function is
$\lambda$-Lipschitz with respect to the actions of the other players. They
showed that such games admit $\epsilon$-approximate pure Nash equilibria for
certain settings of $\epsilon$ and $\lambda$. They left open, however, the
question of how hard it is to find such an equilibrium. In this work, we
develop a query-efficient reduction from more general games to Lipschitz games.
We use this reduction to show a query lower bound for any randomized algorithm
finding $\epsilon$-approximate pure Nash equilibria of $n$-player,
binary-action, $\lambda$-Lipschitz games that is exponential in
$\frac{n\lambda}{\epsilon}$. In addition, we introduce ``Multi-Lipschitz
games,'' a generalization involving player-specific Lipschitz values, and
provide a reduction from finding equilibria of these games to finding
equilibria of Lipschitz games, showing that the value of interest is the sum of
the individual Lipschitz parameters. Finally, we provide an exponential lower
bound on the deterministic query complexity of finding $\epsilon$-approximate
correlated equilibria of $n$-player, $m$-action, $\lambda$-Lipschitz games,
valid for all $\lambda \geq 1$ and $\epsilon \leq 1$.
  Our lower bounds build upon a new approach to the classic problem of finding
an approximate Nash equilibrium. We say that a problem setting gives rise to a
``Nash hardness'' parameter $\gamma$ if every deterministic algorithm for it
must consider the action of every other player when determining the next
action to suggest to the focal player of the query. We define $\gamma$ formally
and show that lower bounds on $\gamma$ imply lower bounds on the query
complexity of all randomized algorithms for finding an $\epsilon$-approximate
Nash equilibrium.

a popular method for estimating the true
performance of machine learning models, allowing model selection and parameter
tuning. However, the very process of CV requires random partitioning of the
data and so our performance estimates are in fact stochastic, with variability
that can be substantial for natural language processing tasks. We demonstrate
that these unstable estimates cannot be relied upon for effective parameter
tuning. The resulting tuned parameters are not stable across different
partitionings of the data, leading to a situation where we are essentially
tuning different models each time we perform tuning. We explore a number of
practical solutions to this problem, including the use of a single partition
of the data, hyperparameter sampling, and a new method we call "CV without
shuffling." We evaluate these approaches on a large and diverse dataset of 201
datasets that we have made available for use.
  Our evaluation demonstrates that the simplest solution -- not shuffling the
data before performing CV gives performance estimates that are essentially
deterministic, removing the need for multiple partitionings. This approach is
also much faster than typical k-fold CV, making it thousands of times more
practical for tuning parameters.
  We argue that the safe default is to not shuffle the data before performing
CV, removing the need for multiple partitionings and the associated variability
of performance estimates. To this end, we update the CV function to the new
default of "CV without shuffling," which is simple to implement and removes the
need for any further modification on the part of users.
  Finally, we demonstrate that this new default gives us a number of other
benefits, including the ability to evaluate the significance of performance
gains due to different features (e.g., gender, race), and a way to regulate
such gains in order to avoid unfair models. We hope that others will find these
tools as useful as we do.

aware of the potential impact of algorithmic biases on their ability to
retrieve all relevant information, and how much relevant information may
actually be missed due to Web search personalisation. We find that the majority
of participants in our experimental study are neither aware that there is a
potential problem nor do they have a strategy to mitigate the risk of missing
relevant information when performing online searches. Using a within-study
design, we also find that using DuckDuckGo as a comparison search engine can
yield different results for search terms that are relevant to the professional
work of public sector officials. Our findings have practical implications for
the development of strategies that can help public sector officials to retrieve
all relevant information, and, more broadly, to effectively perform online
searches in the service of their professional work.

fluid propagation (CFP) is introduced. Processes in a CFP are enabled and
preemptively fired in a fluid manner; they try to bind to incoming constraints
while allowing for overbinding. The outcome of the binding is checked dynamically
by the process and an option to propagate the bound constraint further is
provided. A CFP language based on CSP-like syntax is developed; its semantics

notion of CF-approximation spaces. A CFP library for the Janus framework is also

discussed; a CCS-like language, Con Constraint, is introduced as a version of

trying of constraints by processes; it is shown that the standard CCP semantics
is recovered by considering CF-approximation spaces.

and a denotational one are presented for this framework. Concurrent fluid
propagation is introduced as a CCS-like language; no concurrency primitives are
present, but concurrency arises from the concurrent trying of constraints by
processes. It is shown that the standard CCP semantics is recovered by
considering CF-approximation spaces.

a vital role in developing NLP systems to provide confidence that the
difference in performance between two systems (i.e., the test statistic) is not
due to luck. However, practitioners rely on Monte Carlo approximation to
perform this test due to a lack of a suitable exact algorithm. In this work,
we provide an efficient exact algorithm for the paired-permutation test for a
family of structured test statistics. Our algorithm runs in $\mathcal{O}(GN

the Monte Carlo approximation with $20000$ samples on a common dataset.

larger set of permutations, which yields a p-value that is $11 \%$ more
conservative when the null hypothesis is true.

corruption.

which is more flexible and easier to be implemented. Finally, we discuss the
proposed GraphCorruption framework is superior over existing adversarial attack
approaches for GNNs, and give a state-of-the-art attack success rate on various
GNN models.

trustworthiness of GNNs by adapting both node features and graph connections to
attack GNNs, and it has the potential of being used as a white box adversary to
evaluate the robustness of GNNs and to train more robust GNN models.

comprehensive evaluation framework for GNNs and natural systems (e.g,

the aggregate flexibility, which consider both heterogeneous loads and
weather forecasting errors. The first algorithm uses a two-stage approach,

novel technique (to our knowledge) of modeling the road layout as a Markov Chain

for the traffic) in a sequence to generate the overall traffic scene. We present
state-of-the-art results both for road layout generation and traffic generation.

interest that our model is using to make the prediction and show that they are

reasonability of our solution and also to compare with the prior work (Deep in

3D detection (Far3Det) of objects beyond a
certain distance from an observer, e.g., $>$50m. Far3Det is particularly
important for autonomous vehicles (AVs) operating at highway speeds, which
require detections of far-field obstacles to ensure sufficient braking
distances. However, contemporary Far3Det algorithms are mainly developed using
simulated data, and there is a general perception that they will not work as
well on real-world data due to realistic complexities such as lie-scale
biases. On the other hand, contemporary object detection algorithms on real
imagery perform far better than dedicated Far3Det algorithms, raising the
question of whether dedicated Far3Det algorithms are even necessary on real
data. To answer this question, we start by collecting a real-world dataset of
video and lidar recordings spanning about 8,500 miles, and annotate 312,812
frames with bounding box annotations. We then compare two types of models:
(1) dedicated Far3Det models trained on simulated data and fine-tuned on
our real dataset, and (2) baseline models representing the current state-of-the-
art 3D detection models on real data. We find that baseline models perform
nearly as well as dedicated Far3Det models on this data, making dedicated Far3Det
algorithms for real-world scenarios questionable.
  We also observe lieness (lie-scale bias) in real detection, where objects
are under-detected or over-detected based on their distance from the camera.
Dedicated Far3Det algorithms trained on simulated data reflect this lieness
and perform worse on real data relative to baseline models, see Figure 2,
which shows that even dedicated Far3Det algorithms can be fooled by lieness.
Finally, we also find that while lidar sensors can improve 3D detection on
real data, dedicated Far3Det algorithms do no better than baseline models on
data involving lidar sensors, see Figure 3. Therefore, the benefit of dedicated
Far3Det algorithms on real data, if any, is not worth the cost of training
such algorithms.
  We conclude with evidence that 3D detection on real data is already pretty
good and does not need dedicated Far3Det algorithms. We release our dataset
available at https://yann042.github.io/Far3Det/.

energized by a DEN-derived stiffness tensor. Both are registered using
conjugate gradients with a shared surface. Experimental results demonstrate
that the proposed methods outperform the DEN on various liver and brain
datasets both visually and numerically.

to the fixed membrane. Both are compared to a classical rigid registration
method. Results show that adding integrated RBTs improves the registration
accuracy significantly, while the second approach is not as beneficial. Both
methods are computationally more expensive than the baseline DEN, but similar to
a rigid registration.

fluorescence imaging. We register a rigid transformation to a flexible
non-rigid deformation and evaluate the effect of adding RBTs. Our results
demonstrate that the approaches that include RBTs outperform the baseline
non-rigid registration both visually and numerically.

produce tight filters for programs written in interpreted languages such as

we investigate the effect of the frame rate of the input video on the
performance of the transcoding process when the H.264 video transcoding
algorithm is utilized on the heterogeneous cloud VMs. Our analysis reveals
that while the frame rate of the input video does not affect the performance on
all VM types, it has a significant influence on the performance on the Medium

transcoding on the Medium VM type, the input video needs to be split into
segments with a consideration of the frame rate. This phenomenon can help
cloud providers to offer frame rate transcoding services with a guarantee on
the completion time (ie, to transcode a video with a specific frame rate) and
enable SSPs to effectively utilize cloud services to meet the streaming

  We show that a transverse solitary wave is an orbit of a hyperbolic,

constant. By using the Cole--Hopf transformation, we reduce the study of the
spectral and orbital stability of solitary wave to that of the spectral and
orbital stability of periodic traveling wave of a parabolic equation in
infinite phase space. By using the minimization of the action functional on
the appropriate invariant manifolds, we then obtain that the periodic
traveling wave is spectrally and orbitally stable if the anharmonic oscillator
constant is positive, and that it is unstable if it is negative.

symplectic manifold equipped with the kinetic momentum as a symplectic form, and
also that of the determining equations of solitary wave and periodic traveling
wave.

orbital stability of solitary wave depends on the choice of the potential of the
anharmonic oscillator. A paper on the generalization of these results to the

the neuroepithelium before the emergence of ganglion cells. Here, we use
two-photon and lightsheet imaging of the zebrafish retina $in~vivo$ to
investigate the behavior of the mitotic spindle during this period. We show
that the orientation of the spindle is randomly distributed with respect to
the radial axis of the retina but systematically correlated with the position
of the nucleus within the epithelium. We further show that this correlation is
due to a systematic change in the orientation of the spindle in response to

theoretical explanation for the end point of the pseudogap in the (T, x) phase
diagram and the enhanced nematic susceptibility in a wide range of temperatures
and doping levels.
  We propose that the exceptional van Hove singularity is the key to understanding
the pseudogap of YBa$_2$Cu$_3$O$_{7-\delta}$ (YBCO). Using a two-dimensional
hubbard model with asymmetric bands we access an end point on the antiferromagnetic
sine-Gordon ladder that is proximate to a second order van Hove singularity.
Activation of spin density waves is tied to the exceptional van Hove singularity:
it is switched on at a temperature $T^{*}$, and switched off as $T \rightarrow
0$. $T^*$ is tuned by doping, and in the optimally doped sample, it is
extrapolated to zero doping level. Below $T^*$, the sin-Gordon ladder is
split into two separate rungs, which gives rise to a "pseudogap" for electrons
of any orientation. $T^*$ coincides with the onset of nematic susceptibility
and specific heat peak. The theoretical picture is challenged by a
spin-echo decay experiment, which measures the spin gap. We explain the
experimental findings by proposing that the spin gap measured in the experiment
is the gap on the upper branch of the split Fermi surface. We call this gap the
"Fermi gap" and show that it is much smaller than the pseudogap.

TESS have demonstrated that
planets are ubiquitous. However, the success of these missions heavily depends
on ground-based radial velocity (RV) surveys, which combined with transit
photometry can yield bulk densities and orbital properties. While most Kepler
host stars are too faint for detailed follow-up observations, TESS is detecting
planets orbiting nearby bright stars that are more amenable to RV
characterization. Here we introduce the TESS-Keck Survey (TKS), an RV program
using ~100 nights on Keck/HIRES to study exoplanets identified by TESS. The
primary survey aims are investigating the link between stellar properties and
the compositions of small planets; studying how the diversity of system
architectures depends on dynamical configurations or planet multiplicity;
identifying prime candidates for atmospheric studies with JWST; and
understanding the role of stellar evolution in shaping planetary systems. We
present a fully-automated target selection algorithm, which yielded 103 planets
in 86 systems for the final TKS sample. Most TKS hosts are inactive,
solar-like, main-sequence stars (4500 K < Teff < 6000 K) at a wide range of
metallicities. The selected TKS sample contains 71 small planets (Rp < 4 Re),
11 systems with multiple transiting candidates, 6 sub-day period planets and 3
planets in the habitable zone of their hosts. The TKS sample includes 3 planets
with durations of transit eclipses longer than their orbital periods (transit
eclipses occur when the planet orbits a star rotating at less than half the
planetary orbital period; hereafter "long-eclipse periods" planets), which are
exceptional because the orbital and stellar periods are not in a simple
multiples relationship.

is uncorrelated with stellar rotation period, but strongly correlated with the
stellar rotation rate (as inferred from the host activity level). As a result,
we suggest that the incidence of long-eclipse periods is less than 1% for
planets in systems where the stellar rotation rate is greater than ~0.5 d^{-1}.
We also propose an empirical approach to estimate the orbital period of
non-transiting inner planets and better characterize their place in the system
architecture.

years. While Instagram allows users to express their opinions through
capabilities such as comments and likes, it also provides an opportunity for
spammers. Several spam types exist in Instagram, including comment spam,
message spam, and bio spam. Due to the complexity of Instagram's API policies,
existing anti-comment-spam techniques cannot be fully utilized to automatically
remove and filter comment spammers on Instagram. To address this problem, in
this paper, we propose an algorithm called THRESHOLD that can be used by any
Instagram user to automatically remove and filter comment spammers. The
algorithm was tested using the comment data obtained from the Instagram
account of one of the authors. The results show that the proposed algorithm
produced excellent performance in terms of accuracy, precision, recall, and
F1-score, even when it faced noisy data. We also show that the algorithm is
scalable and efficient in terms of running time.
  We also find that the number of comments (which is also known as --footprint-- in
social media) is the most important feature to determine comment spammers.
Therefore, our algorithm thresholds the number of comments to filter spam
comments. We call this approach the Footprint Thresholding approach. Footprint
Thresholding is easy to implement, efficient in terms of running time, scalable
over datasets of different sizes, and works well on datasets with noisy data.
Furthermore, Footprint Thresholding is a content-agnostic approach that does not
require natural language processing techniques to analyze the content of the
comment, thus making it faster than other content-analyzing approaches.
Finally, we propose and test two filtering strategies: the Random
Sampling strategy and the Popularity Filtering strategy. The Results show that
both strategies produce promising results, but with some limitations.
Nonetheless, due to its simplicity and efficiency, we recommend using the
algorithm in conjunction with both filtering strategies.

result of independent interest proved by Yehuda Shalom and myself which says
that if a group acts properly and transively on a Roelcke precompact metric
space then it is bound to have a certain subgroup isomorphic to itself. This
result generalises a result proved by myself alone for the case of a group
acting on a compact space.

necessary and that the statements of our theorems cannot be strengthened.

stellar astrophysics
and exoplanetary science. In the M-dwarf regime, much effort has gone into
defining empirical relations that can use readily accessible observables to
assess physical stellar properties. Often, these relations for the quantity of
interest are cast as a non-linear function of available data; however, in
Bayesian modeling the reverse is needed. In this article, we introduce a new
Bayesian framework to self-consistently and simultaneously apply multiple
empirical calibrations to fully characterize the mass, luminosity, radius, and
effective temperature of a field age M-dwarf. This framework includes a new
M-dwarf mass-radius relation with a scatter of 3.1% at fixed mass. We further
introduce the M-dwarf Ultraviolet Spectroscopic Sample (MUSS), and apply our
methodology to provide consistent stellar parameters for these nearby low-mass
stars, which are primarily known for their H I absorption lines that are used as
orbital tracers for exoplanets in sub-au scales. Using the spectroscopic
sample, we evaluate the empirical relations for mass, radius, and effective
temperature, and provide guidelines for proper calibration and usage. We find
no significant bias in the estimated ages, but a minor bias (less than 0.03 dex)
in the estimated luminosities and effective temperatures. We further report on
the dependence of the MUSS relations on metallicity and stellar activity, and
find that while the trends are present, the scatter in the relations dominates
the uncertainties in the mean. Finally, we discuss the importance of
self-consistently estimating the stellar parameters when analyzing exoplanet
candidates, and provide stellar parameters for 16 planets whose hosts are part
of the MUSS sample.

data set with spatial locations, how can we efficiently enumerate objects within

generalization of a algorithm by Chen et al. for k=2, and a new reduction for

parameters, and computed the marginal likelihood of the overdispersal parameter
\omega. We then used this to compute a Bayes factor, which we found to be a
more intuitive measure of the significance of \omega than the marginal likelihood
itself. Finally, we used this approach to fit a model to early UK COVID-19 data,
finding that the data shows a significant effect of the overdispersal factor at
the early stages of the epidemic.

$\omega=1$ to one with $\omega\approx10$, indicating that the data shows a
significant effect of the overdispersal factor at the early stages of the
epidemic. Furthermore, we find that fixing $\omega$ at its estimated value
results in a model that accurately fits the reported number of deaths rather
than the reported number of infections, suggesting that care must be taken when
applying models which estimate $\omega$ from infection data to death data.
Finally, we estimate that the "superspreading events" explained 44\% of the
variance in the number of infections (and 80\% of the variance in the number

the status of requirements engineering
in the gaming industry. Recent papers in the area were surveyed.
Characterizations of the gaming industry were deliberated upon by portraying
its relations with the market industry category. Some research directions in the
area of requirements engineering in the gaming industry were also mentioned.
Finally, a research agenda in this area is proposed.
  In the market industry, service-oriented is the prevailing business model.
We characterize the gaming industry as a service-oriented market industry that
provides entertainment services to its customers. We then relate the gaming
industry to other market industries and propose a socio-technical framework for
its service development. Requirements engineering in the gaming industry is
then discussed with this framework in mind. The framework is also useful in
bridging the gap between the business and technical aspects of the gaming
industry.
  Several characterization efforts are surveyed in the area of the gaming
industry. Each of them is then related to its underlying assumptions and
boundary definitions. For instance, the gaming industry is characterized as a
design industry. It is then related to the service industry and its design
process. The engineering of the gaming system is then seen as a service design
for entertaining experiences. The notion of design in the gaming industry is
then elaborated upon with its scientific and artisanal sides. The artisanal side
of design in the gaming industry is then related to the artcraft in software
development.
  Three approaches to engineering the gaming system are then reviewed. They are
all based on the concept of service in the gaming industry. The difference
between them lies in the scope of services, from the single game to the
enterprise of gaming. The need for enterprise architecture in the gaming
industry is then highlighted. A systemic approach to the enterprise architecture
for the gaming industry is then proposed. It is built around the concept of
service entering into life cycles. The enterprise architecture for the gaming
industry is then presented as a framework for service-oriented enterprise
development.
  Finally, a research agenda for requirements engineering in the gaming industry
is proposed. It is built around four research themes: gaming enterprise
architecture, service engineering for entertainment, human-computer
interaction, and business models. The following sub-themes are also suggested:
design science, enterprise architecture, requirements engineering, human-
computer interaction, business models, and sociology. The proposed research
agenda is then a mix of engineering and social scientific studies in the gaming
industry.

descent (DPSGD) is a fundamental challenge. Unlike the typical SGD, private
datasets cannot be used many times for hyperparameter search in DPSGD; e.g.,
via a grid search. Therefore, there is an essential need for algorithms that,
within a given search space, can find near-optimal hyperparameters for the best
achievable privacy-utility tradeoffs efficiently. We formulate this problem
into a general optimization framework for establishing a desirable
privacy-utility tradeoff, and systematically study three cost-effective
algorithms for being used in the proposed framework: evolutionary, Bayesian,
and reinforcement learning. Our experiments, for hyperparameter tuning in DPSGD
conducted on MNIST and CIFAR-10 datasets, show that these three algorithms
significantly outperform the widely used grid search, in terms of both the
quality of the found hyperparameters and the search time. As this is the first
study of hyperparameter tuning in DPSGD, we provide a comprehensive framework
for evaluating such algorithms, and suggest guidelines for algorithm
implementation, making our work a stepping stone for future research in this
domain.

and horizontal privacy and returns as an output a private neural network that
is equivalent to the one that would be learned if all the data were available
in one place and without a need for any additional data publication. Our
protocol achieves (eps, delta)-local differential privacy at the individual
client level and (\epsilon, delta)-compositional differential privacy at the
federated level, for any desired \epsilon, \delta, and we also show how to
achieve end-to-end privacy guarantee. We also show that our protocol is

sketching techniques; and it also achieves better test accuracy than prior
works (which happen because we directly learn a model that is useful on a

suggests that an additional source of nitrogen enrichment, beyond that provided

Virus Disease 2019 (COVID-19) pandemic swept the
world.In China, COVID-19 has caused severe consequences. Moreover, online
rumors during the COVID-19 pandemic increased people's panic about public
health and social stability. At present, understanding and curbing the spread
of online rumors is an urgent task. Therefore, we analyzed the rumor spreading
mechanism and propose a method to quantify a rumors' influence by the speed of
new insiders. The search frequency of the rumor is used as an observation
variable of new insiders. The peak coefficient and the attenuation coefficient
are calculated for the search frequency, which conforms to the exponential
distribution. We designed several rumor features and used the above two
coefficients as predictable labels. A 5-fold cross-validation experiment using
the mean square error (MSE) as the loss function showed that the decision tree
was suitable for predicting the peak coefficient, and the linear regression
model was ideal for predicting the attenuation coefficient. Our feature
analysis showed that precursor features were the most important for the
outbreak coefficient, while location information and rumor entity information
were the most important for the attenuation coefficient. Meanwhile, features
that were conducive to the outbreak were usually harmful to the continued
spread of rumors. At the same time, anxiety was a crucial rumor causing factor.
Finally, we discuss how to use deep learning technology to reduce the forecast
loss by a external branch.
  Our code is attached to this paper, which can be downloaded from
https://github.com/Chen56666/COVID-19-rumor.
  The paper is organized as follows: In Section 2, the rumor spreading mechanism
is analyzed, and the outbreak and attenuation coefficients are defined. In
Section 3, the prediction models for the above coefficients are introduced.
Section 4 contains feature analysis. In Section 5, the forecast loss is
discussed, and the prospects for improving forecasting performance are
expated.
  As the COVID-19 pandemic continues to spread, online rumors are becoming an
increasingly relevant problem ^{1} ^{2} ^{3}. Therefore, scientific
research on rumor spreading and development is of great significance for the
prevention of COVID-19 and the maintenance of social stability. In this paper,
we analyze the rumor spreading mechanism and propose a method to quantify a
rumor's influence by the speed of new insiders. The search frequency of the
rumor is used as an observation variable of new insiders.

chanical modeling of the
strain-induced crystallization in unfilled polymers. This phenomenon
significantly influences mechanical and thermal properties of polymers and has
to be taken into consideration when planning manufacturing processes as well as
applications of the final product. In order to simultaneously capture both
kinds of effects, the model proposed starts by introducing a triple
decomposition of the deformation gradient and furthermore uses thermodynamic
framework for material modeling based on the Coleman--Noll procedure and
minimum principle of the dissipation potential, which requires suitable
assumptions for the Helmholtz free energy and the dissipation potential. The
chosen setup yields evolution equations which are able to simulate the
formation and the degradation of crystalline regions as well as the
orientation of crystalline and amorphous regions. The presented model is
employed in a finite element framework in order to simulate a compression
test and to investigate the mechanical as well as thermal properties of a
polymer sample. The obtained results show that the proposed model is able to
simulate the formation of crystals during the process and thus provides a
reasonable description of the sample behavior both with respect to
mechanical and thermal effects.

model, phase-field model, finite element simulation.

calculate the Zeeman part of magnetic susceptibility for nematic and chiral
superconducting phases near T$_c$ in Ginzburg-Landau formalism. Superconducting
order parameter from $E_u$ representation has non-trivial coupling with the
transversal Zeeman field that results in a paramagnetic response of the
magnetic susceptibility. The results are explained by the presence of magnetic
ipochronicity - a change of sign of the mixing of superconducting and magnetic
fields under spatial inversion.
  We propose that the paramagnetic response near T$_c$ could be a benchmark for
experimental detection of nematic superconductivity in doped topological insulators.
It could also be compared to existing theoretical predictions for magnetic
susceptibility in iron-selenide superconductors.
  Let us note that in contrast to iron-selenides, doped topological insulators
have relatively small carrier bandwidth. This results in a qualitative change
of the phase diagram with increasing carrier density: from a chiral to a
non-chiral (nematic) superconducting state. This change is induced by tuning
of the superconducting order parameter to couple to the spatial inversion symmetry.
Therefore, study of the magnetization effects in this system provides a unique
probe for nematic superconductivity.

have not contact with superconductivity and topological insulators. Detailed
explanations of underlying physics, mathematical derivations and references

possibility of exciting orbital
out-of-phase oscillations in binary black hole systems, which depends on the
orbital eccentricity and the compactness of the binaries. In the context of
standard general relativity, the effect of this coupling on the gravitational
wave (GW) emission has been found to be relatively small. However, alternative
theories of gravity give rise to different effective gravitational potentials
and hence different effective profiles of orbital eccentricity and orbital
expansion in the different theories. In this work, we investigate the role of
inter-orbital coupling in $f(R)$-theory binaries, and find that it can be
considerably larger in $f(R)$-theory than in general relativity, depending on
the form of the $f(R)$ function. Moreover, we find that this coupling can
result in a significant modification to the GW signal due to a frequency
shift. In particular, we find that the effect of inter-orbital coupling on the
GW signal can be distinguished from that of orbital oscillations in
non-eccentric binaries by a signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) of $\sim 10$ with
third-generation GW detectors for some $f(R)$-theory models.
  Furthermore, we find that the merged waveform can be qualitatively different
in the intermediate stage of the merger between $f(R)$-theory and general
relativity. This could provide a means of distinguishing $f(R)$-theory from
general relativity in future GW observations.
  We also investigate the effect of inter-orbital coupling on the ringdown
emission of binary black hole mergers in $f(R)$-theory. We find that this
effect can be considerably larger in $f(R)$-theory than in general relativity,
and may provide a means of distinguishing different $f(R)$-theory models. In
particular, we find that the quasinormal oscillations can be damped in a
non-universal way in $f(R)$-theory.
  Our study indicates that investigating the effect of inter-orbital coupling
in GW observations of eccentric binaries is important for testing alternative
theories of gravity.

the combined field of two optical (or near-optical) lasers and compare various

diffraction and birefringence, special emphasis is placed on scenarios where

assumed, whereas no such restrictions are placed on the strength of the two
optical lasers. Further assumptions on the initial state of the x-ray photon
are not made. Therefore the calculations comprise transitions between
non-classical x-ray states. The transition probabilities and Stokes parameters
are calculated for the situation where the x-ray photon travels in a
low-density atomic gas (e.g. helium). In a solid (e.g. sodium), also the
electronic response is studied.

resources available at HIBEF, the probability for single photon transitions
should be on a detectable level for the scenario of forward scattering of
perpendicular polarizations. For all other scenarios, including those with
non-collinear scattering, an enhancement of the x-ray flux by approximately an
order of magnitude would be necessary.

detection methods should be available for an observation of quantum
birefringence.

Broadbent and Lord (TQC'20), is an
encryption scheme with the following attractive feature: given a ciphertext, an
adversary cannot create two ciphertexts both of which decrypt to the same
message as the original ciphertext. We revisit this notion and show the
following:
  - Reusability: The constructions proposed by Broadbent and Lord have the
disadvantage that they either guarantee one-time security (that is, the
encryption key can only be used once to encrypt the message) in the plain model
or they guaranteed security in the random oracle model. We construct unclonable
encryption schemes with semantic security. We present two constructions (for
public-key and private-key settings) from minimal cryptographic assumptions.
  - Lower Bound and Generalized Construction: We revisit the
information-theoretic one-time secure construction of Broadbent and Lord. The
success probability of the adversary in their construction was guaranteed to be
$0.85^n$, where $n$ is the length of the message. It was interesting to
understand whether the ideal success probability of (negligibly close to)
$0.5^n$ was unattainable. We generalize their construction to be based on a
broader class of monogamy of entanglement games. We demonstrate a simple
cloning attack that succeeds with probability $0.71^n$ against a class of
schemes (not exclusive to) constructed using this framework.
  - Composable Security: All of the constructions mentioned above are of one-time
secure. Guaranteeing composable security (where the security reduction
simulation belongs to a broad class of efficient simulations, and not just a
passive simulation as in traditional security definitions) is more challenging.

assumptions a scheme guaranteeing this security definition.

and composable setting all live in the computational model (assuming minimal
hardness assumptions). Our one-time and composable constructions also
generalize previous constructions of unclonable encryption.

be used to perform
information-theoretic authentication in additive white Gaussian noise channels,
as long as the adversary is not omniscient. The model considered consists of an
encoder, decoder, and adversary, where the adversary has access to the message,
a non-causal noisy observation of the encoder's transmission, and unlimited
transmission power, while the decoder observes a noisy version of the sum of
the encoder and adversary's outputs. A method to modify a generic existing
channel code to enable authentication is presented. It is shown that this
modification costs an asymptotically negligible amount of the coding rate,
while still enabling authentication as long as the adversary's observation is
not noiseless. Also notable is that this modification is not (asymptotically) a
function of the statistical characterization of the adversary's channel and
furthermore no secret key is required, hence paving the way for a robust
practical implementation. Using these results, the channel-authenticated
capacity is calculated and shown to be equal to the non-adversarial channel
capacity. While this modular scheme is designed for use in the given channel
model, it is applicable to a wide range of settings.
  This work builds off of a modification of the Tal-Ianacccone scheme which
was designed to counter an all powerful adversary who knows the message,
strategy of the encoder and entire trajectory of the decoder's received signal.
The scheme developed here is applicable to a more realistic robustness
setting, showing that authentication is possible even when the adversary has
access to the message and non-finite but still noisy observation of the
encoder's transmission. The ideas presented here are broad and could be
applied to other settings to provide authentication in channels with adverse
party interference.

combination of interband transitions and doping play important roles in

effects of mass transfer and mass outflow.

Lipschitz continuity of
neural networks with respect to their inputs. To this end, we provide a simple
technique for computing an upper bound to the Lipschitz constant---for multiple
$p$-norms---of a feed forward neural network composed of commonly used layer
types. Our technique is then used to formulate training a neural network with a
bounded Lipschitz constant as a constrained optimisation problem that can be
solved using projected stochastic gradient methods. Our evaluation study shows
that the performance of the resulting models exceeds that of models trained
with other common regularisers. We also provide evidence that the
hyperparameters are intuitive to tune, demonstrate how the choice of norm for
computing the Lipschitz constant impacts the resulting model, and show that the
performance gains provided by our method are particularly noticeable when only
a small amount of training data is available.
