  We focus on the task of agreement prediction in Basque, as a case study for a
task that requires implicit understanding of sentence structure and the
acquisition of a complex but consistent morphological system. Analyzing
experimental results from two syntactic prediction tasks -- verb number
prediction and suffix recovery -- we find that sequential models perform worse
on agreement prediction in Basque than one might expect on the basis of a
previous agreement prediction work in English. We argue that English-style
agreement models are able to blind out the hierarchical structure of sentences,
while failing to learn the structure of the Basque case system. Low performance
is thus due to a failure to understand the hierarchical structure of sentences
as much as the grammatical system of Basque itself.
  To empirically support our claim we train a model to predict Basque case
markers given sentences in which all other words are filled in dummy case.
We find that even in this setup the model struggles to learn to predict case on
the noun directly adjacent to the verb, indicating that local features
dominate over contextual ones. This is in contrast to a version of the task
in which all nouns are filled in dummy case, in which the model learns to
predict case on all nouns in the sentence. We argue that duality of Basque
nouns -- being both subjects and objects -- make the agreement system more
similar to that of English, and make it a promising target for future work.
  Overall, agreement prediction in Basque provides a challenging test case for
sequential models which it fails. We argue that, contrary to common
interpretations, the low performance is due to a lack of understanding of the
hierarchical structure of sentences combined with a struggle to grasp the
Basque case system.

  Let $f$ be a function from directed acyclic graphs (DAGs) to the set $\{
yes,no,don't\ know\}$. We define $f$-upward planarity testing ($f$-UP, for
short) as the problem of deciding whether a DAG is upward planar with respect
to $f$, that is, whether it admits an upward planar drawing and the number of
sources (outlets) with three initial edges is less than $f$.
  We obtain new fixed-parameter algorithms parameterized by the number of
sources, treedepth and vertex cover. All three algorithms are obtained using a
novel framework for the problem that combines SPQR tree-decompositions with
parameterized techniques. Our approach unifies and pushes beyond previous
tractability results for the problem on series-parallel digraphs, single-source
digraphs and outerplanar digraphs.
  We also show that the problem is W[1]-hard parameterized by treedepth, for
which we give an XP-algorithm parameterized by this parameter.
  Finally, we determine the complexity of the problem with respect to the
number of sources under various restrictions on the structure of the input
digraph.

parameters, precision long-baseline
neutrino oscillation experiments rely on detailed models of neutrino
interactions with nuclei. These models constitute an important source of
systematic uncertainty, partially because detectors to date have been blind to
final state neutrons. Three-dimensional projection scintillator trackers
comprise components of the near detectors of the next generation long-baseline
neutrino experiments. Due to the good timing resolution and fine granularity,
this technology is capable of measuring neutron kinetic energy in neutrino
interactions on an event-by-event basis and will provide valuable data for
refining neutrino interaction models and ways to reconstruct neutrino energy.
Two prototypes have been exposed to the neutron beamline at Los Alamos National
Laboratory (LANL) in both 2019 and 2020, with neutron energies between 0 and
800 MeV. In order to demonstrate the capability of neutron detection, the total
neutron-scintillator cross section is measured and compared to external
measurements. The measured total neutron cross section in scintillator between
98 and 688 MeV is 0.36 $\pm$ 0.05 barn.
  In addition to the total cross section, the fine timing information allows
the easy identification of the neutron time-distribution in neutrino events and
the separation of neutron and proton scattering events. The average neutron
time-after-meson is between 40 and 100 ns for all available neutron energies.
Neutron-proton (n-p) final states are easily distinguished from heavier
fragments by the time-of-flight and kinetic energy. The n-p separation efficiency
is 80% for energies above 100 MeV.
  The proton time-in-flight and kinetic energy measurements confirm the
reliability of the neutron detectors and set the stage for neutron reconstruction
accuracy validation and neutrino interaction study with multiple final state
particles.
  In conclusion, the good performance of the neutron detection with 3D
projection scintillator trackers is demonstrated and will contribute to
refining neutrino interaction models for improved neutrino energy
reconstruction.

temperature dependence of
sticking forces between micrometer grains of chondritic composition. The data
showed a decrease in surface energy by a factor ~5 with increasing temperature.
Here, we focus on the effect of surface water on grains. Under ambient
conditions in the laboratory, multiple water layers are present. At the low
pressure of protoplanetary discs and for moderate temperatures, grains likely
only hold a monolayer. As dust drifts inwards, even this monolayer eventually
evaporates completely in higher temperature regions. To account for this, we
measured the tensile strength for the same chondritic material as was prepared
and measured for fracture and sticking under various relative humidity levels.
The result shows a factor ~20 increase in surface energy when compared to
standard laboratory conditions. When combined with previous results, the
correction for the effect of water leads to a factor ~3 increase in surface
energy with increasing temperature. This strongly increases the likelihood that
stickiness is the cause for gravitational collapse in protoplanetary dust
cores.
  We also report a tensile strength 1000 times weaker than previously
measured. This challenges the use of this value as a proxy for the strength of
protoplanetary dust aggregates (like in models for dust grains growth and
drift). The small tensile strength (about 1 Pa) may be of importance for
exoplanet atmospheres (e.g., exoplanet inflation) and the formation of chondritic
meteorites.
  Finally, the high surface energy in the presence of water together with the
low tensile strength make the sticking under wet conditions an interesting
environment to do further laboratory research about dust growth and grain
drift.
  Based on the large uncertainty in the temperature dependence of the sticking
forces, the results presented here do not directly impact our previously
published models for dust growth and drift. When future laboratory results are
available, these models will need to be updated.

generation, imitation learning has been viewed as a vital direction in the
context of robot skill learning. In contrast to unconstrained imitation
learning which ignores possible internal and external constraints arising from
environments and robot kinematics/dynamics, recent works on constrained
imitation learning allow for transferring human skills to unstructured
scenarios and improving the overall performance. This paper provides a comprehensive survey on constrained imitation learning, detailing both
built-in constraints during the learning phase and external constraints on the
data. We categorize constraints into kinematic, dynamic, and physical
constraints, and propose a unified framework for handling these constraints.
Besides, we discuss different algorithms addressing constraint imitation learning
and evaluate the performance of these algorithms on specific tasks. With a
comprehensive survey of the field of constraint imitation learning, this
work provides a theoretical foundation for developing novel algorithms handling
more types of constraints, and helps to evaluate the effectiveness of
state-of-the-art algorithms, thereby guiding the improvement of future
applications.

width of a brush is always bounded from below, a feature that is particularly
relevant in the limit of strong stretching where end-to-end segment separations
vary over a large range. Recent theoretical developments have shown that this
boundedness gives rise to a phenomenon of competition between polymer brushes
in which the presence of one brush affects the adsorption free energy of
subsequent brushes; thus, the adsorption behavior of the system cannot be
reduced to that of non-interacting brushes. Here, we focus on the adsorbed
amount, rather than the free energy, and provide a theory for adsorbed polymers
in the strongly stretched regime by modifying the mapping from monomer to a
harmonic oscillator. Unlike the parabolic brush limit, our mapping takes into
account the boundedness of the brush, and thus the competition between the
monomers. Consistent with the lack of concurrence between the parabolic and
exact results for the quantity of interest, numerical calculations show that
our results are different from those predicted by the parabolic brush theory.
Moreover, we provide an analytical expression for the adsorbed amount in the
limit of strong stretching and large loop size. Our predictions are generally
higher than those predicted by the parabolic brush theory, which should be of
use for polymer brushes grafted on colloids with a large radius.

choice settings, we explore its usefulness in tackling various combinatorial
optimization problems. We do this by considering an abstract model, in which
a set of agents are asked to act in a particular ordering, called the action
sequence. Each agent acting in the $k^{th}$ position of the sequence receives a
profit of $s_k$ from the action $A_k$. The goal is to compute an action
sequence that maximizes the total profit, also called the social welfare. We
assume a non-tractable preference reporting mechanism and focus on query
complexity of computationally limited agents who can report only a constant
number of bits per query. We establish a tight bound of $\approx 0.69n$ on the
number of queries required by a randomized mechanism achieving a $1-\frac{1}{e}$
approximation of the optimal welfare. To the best of our knowledge, this is the
first such result for nearly-optimal social welfare in an action sequence
settings with non-tractable preferences and constant query complexity.
  Our result also yields a new welfare guarantee for randomized dictatorship
mechanisms in social choice settings with free-riding. We achieve an approximation
of $1-e^{-d/2}$ with query complexity of $O(n/d)$, improving upon the 2-approximation
of Peck and Wang [EC'20], for any positive $d \leq n$.
  Finally, we also give a 1.5-approximation with query complexity of $\approx 0.25n$. The
corresponding randomized mechanism is pure (deterministic) for $n=5,6,7$.
  All of our results hold under the standard assumption of free-riding, where
agents are not charged for their reported preferences.
  The paper introduces a new framework for analyzing query complexity of
mechanisms in settings with free-riding. We hope that our results and approach
will be useful in further investigations of query-efficient social choice
and combinatorial optimization problems.

process is an open and challenging question in biology. Recent studies classify
the topology and geometry of knotted proteins by analysing the distribution of
a protein's planar projections using topological objects called knotoids. We
approach the analysis of proteins with the same topology by introducing a
topologically inspired statistical metric between their knotoid distributions.
We detect geometric differences between trefoil proteins by characterising
their entanglement and we recover a clustering by sequence similarity. By
looking directly at the geometry and topology of their native states, we are
able to probe different folding pathways for proteins forming open-ended
trefoil knots. Interestingly, our pipeline reveals that the folding pathway of
shallow knotted Carbonic Anhydrases involves the creation of a double-looped
structure, differently from what was previously observed for deeply knotted
trefoil proteins. We validate this with Molecular Dynamics simulations.
Finally, our statistical approach allows us to reconstruct the folding pathway
of a knotted Ribonuclease T4, previously studied both experimentally and
computationally. Our results confirm the importance of trefoil knots in
protein evolution and folding and lay the ground for a statistical
characterisation of proteins forming other types of knots.

information including activities, sleep, sports, etc. Smart healthcare achieves
great success by training machine learning models on a large quantity of user
data. However, there are two critical limitations. First, individual models
trained on non-public personal data cannot be combined to get knowledge on
other people. Second, such models are not adaptable to, e.g., temperature and
lightness changes which are common in real-world applications. To address these
problems, we propose a novel universal transfer healthcare network (UTHN) for
combined adaptability. Specifically, we design a network structure with an
encoder-decoder structure and a transferable knowledge layer to combine
individual models. We further propose a range maintenance module (RMM) and a
soft activator (SA) to make the output of the encoder range-adaptive and
private-friendly, respectively. Experiments show that UTNH outperforms
several baseline methods in activity recognition, sleep stage prediction, and
sports duration prediction, with the highest average improvement of 7.41% in
activity recognition, 5.53% in sleep stage prediction, and 10.25% in sports
duration prediction, etc.

This problem studies the model where the same sequence from some set is
transmitted over multiple channels, and the decoder receives the different
outputs. Assume that the transmitted sequence is at distance $d$ from some code
and there are at most $r$ errors in every channel. Then the sequence
reconstruction problem is to find the minimum number of channels required to
recover exactly the transmitted sequence that has to be greater than the
maximum intersection between two metric balls of radius $r$, where the distance
between their centers is at least $d$. In this paper, we study the sequence
reconstruction problem of permutations under the Hamming distance. In this
model, we define a Cayley graph and find the exact value of the largest
intersection of two metric balls in this graph under the Hamming distance for
$r=4$ with $d\geqslant 5$, and for $d=2r$.
  For the specific case of $d=2r$, we also provide a decoding scheme for error
correction codes called homogeneous permutation codes. These codes are
constructed based on the Cayley graph construction. The main feature of these
codes is that the decoder does not have to know which sequence out of a set of
possible transmitted sequences was sent. The decoder has to know only that all
the sequences in this set are from the same set of permutations. Also, the
decoding procedure in this scheme does not require any knowledge of the noise
model.
  The homogeneous permutation codes provide error correction capability up to
$r-1$ errors, and for correcting errors in the transmission process, the
scheme uses $2r$ readings from the channels. It is interesting to note that
the sequence reconstruction problem of permutations for $d=2r$ is equal to $2r$.
Also, for $r=4$ and $d=10$, the largest intersection of two metric balls in
this graph is $940$.

channels.

atom-molecule conversion in spin-1 Bose-Einstein condensates. Specifically, we
discuss how for a suitable dark-state condition the interplay of spin-exchange
collisions and photoassociation leads to the stable creation of an atom-
molecule pairs from three initial spin-zero atoms. This process involves two
two-body interactions and can be intuitively viewed as an effective three-body
recombination. We investigate how the efficiency of this process depends on the
initial temperatures of the condensate and of an applied magnetic field, as
well as on the values of parameters describing the spin-exchange collisions and
the photoassociation. We also study how these parameters influence the
evolution towards an atom-molecule pair state via an intermediate state with
finitely many atoms. Finally, we discuss how the results for the case of an
external magnetic field depend on the choice of spin coherences and on the sign of
the interatomic magnetic moment.

most intriguing phenomena in
modern condensed matter theory. The unique property of having a gap in the
electric charge as well as the topological character makes them promising
candidates for realizing fault-tolerant quantum computing. However, the
generation of chiral charge carriers in topological insulators is a difficult
task. Here, we propose a novel system consisting of a topological insulator
combined with retroreflector layers (e.g. Tungsten Trioxide) and an optically
thin semi-conductor (e.g. Germanium). By applying a circularly polarized laser
we show that in this composite material (known as "meta-topological insulator")
an abundance of massless helical Dirac electrons are created. The created
massless electrons move in the same direction as the light-induced magnetization
and with a speed equal to a fraction of the speed of light. The produced
massless electrons give rise to a DC photocurrent, even when the electric
contacts are non-reversibly oriented with respect to the magnetic field
direction. The DC photocurrent is large (nA scale), easily observable and most
importantly - it persists after the laser is switched off for an extended
period of time. The long persistence is attributed to a trapping of the massless
electrons in the WO$_3$ layers. Our proposal opens a way to create a mass of
massless electrons in a robust and versatile way, which is of great importance
for both fundamental and practical purposes.
  We show that the mass of the massless electrons persists for a considerably
longer time compared to the initial femto-second regime and find two distinct
trapping mechanisms. The first one is due to the trapping of the spin orientation
of the electrons to a stable point of the hysteresis cycle of the refractive
index of WO$_3$. The second mechanism is due to a trapping to localized states
induced by the large lattice distortion in the WO$_3$ layers. The DC photocurrent
is also observable in a magnetic field only if the topological insulator is
combined with a reflector material. We find that the massless electrons are
created on the surface of the topological insulator, but they move in the bulk
of the semiconductor. The mass of the massless electrons persists for a
considerably longer time compared to the initial femto-second regime.

  The present paper is devoted to the resolution of the discrepancy between
non-relativistic and relativistic mean field models concerning the root mean
square radius of the point neutron distribution. In a neutron rich matter, the
interaction of the neutron is expected to be mainly with the neutron. Therefore
the neutron proton effective interaction can be approximately replaced by the
neutron effective interaction. The radius is a low density quantity. Therefore
the Thomas Fermi approximation can be used to further confirm the result
obtained in the finite density framework. The difference between non-relativistic
and relativistic models is then located at the level of the effective mass and
interaction strength. This conclusion contradicts the one reached in a recent
study  for nuclear matter. The values of those quantities in a nuclear
matter are not far from their values in vacuum. Therefore the discrepancy found
in this work for the neutron radius may not be generalized to all quantities.
It should be however noticed that the effective mass of a neutron in a nuclear
medium is expected to be larger than its vacuum value only if the medium
effective interaction is repulsive. The central potential felt by a neutron in
a nuclear medium is expected to be more attractive than its proton counterpart
one. The neutron effective mass is then expected to be smaller than the proton
one, if the repulsion of the one-body potential is mainly due to the
neutron-proton effective interaction. The value of the neutron effective mass in
the model of Adoxado et al.  is larger than expected. It is therefore not
compatible with the data on two neutron system. The discrepancy found in this
work for the neutron radius may also not be generalized to all single particle
properties. It is however expected to be present in the proton radius, which
is also a low density quantity. The spin orbit potential is not present in the
relativistic models used to investigate the neutron radius problem. Therefore an
investigation of its effect on that quantity would be worthwhile.

is a new and important research area in the larger
field of machine learning. With CDL, researchers aim to structure and encode
causal knowledge in the extremely flexible representation space of deep
learning models. Doing so will lead to more robust, generalizable, and
meaningful predictions, which is the ultimate goal in data science. However, to
successfully apply CDL techniques it is crucial to understand the basics,
i.e., the fundamental concepts, techniques, and models. Unfortunately, lacks of
this existent literature and textbook knowledge make it difficult for newcomers
to enter the field of CDL. In this paper, we close this knowledge gap and
provide a comprehensive textbook-style treatment of causal deep learning. We
cover all important concepts, techniques, models, and algorithms, provide
worked-out examples, and offer guidelines on how to conduct CDL research and
projects. Our paper is a must-read for beginners in CDL and serves as a
handbook for experienced researchers in the field.
  We provide a two-fold discussion of CDL. First, we focus on the preparation
for CDL. Here, we cover basic concepts from probability theory and statistics,
and provide an in-depth treatment of causal graphs. Next, we focus on CDL itself
and discuss DAG-based and causal effect models. We provide an exhaustive
treatment of causal graphical models (CGMs) and discuss probabilistic programs
based on CGMs. We focus on Markov Decision Processes (MDPs) and provide a
comprehensive treatment of causal MDPs (CMDPs). Next, we focus on causal
neural network models and discuss causal recurrent neural networks (RNNs) and
long short-term memory (LSTM) architectures. We focus on causal deep
classification models and discuss causal decision support systems based on
deep belief networks (DBNs) and deep policy gradient methods. Finally, we
discuss techniques to learn and use CGMs with deep models and focus on
representation learning with CGMs. We provide an exhaustive treatment of
representations for causal learning and provide a detailed discussion of the
difference between CDL and representation learning. Last but not least, we
discuss the evaluation of CDL models and focus on techniques to validate causal
assumptions in a robust and reliable way. We conclude with a discussion on the
future of CDL and its connections to other important research areas.

concepts,

is crucial for yield optimization and process stability. Yet, in situ
temperature measurements with spatial and temporal resolution are still
challenging. In this work, we perform temperature measurements in a cylindrical
fixed bed reactor by combining the capabilities of real-time magnetic resonance
imaging (MRI) with the temperature-dependent proton resonance frequency (PRF)
shift of water. Three-dimensional (3D) temperature maps are acquired while
heating the bed from room temperature to 60~$^{\circ}$C using hot air. The
obtained results show a clear temperature gradient along the axial and radial
dimensions and agree with optical temperature probe measurements with an
average error of $\pm$ 1.5~$^{\circ}$C. We believe that the MR thermometry
methodology presented here opens the perspective for further quantitative
studies on mass and heat transfer in gas-solid fixed beds and paves the way for
the use of MR as a reference technique for the validation of computational
models. Moreover, the non-invasive nature of MR allows for the future
investigation of the effect of flowing gases on the bed temperature profile and
the evaluation of bed materials with liquid impregnated phases.
  From a methodological point of view, this work shows that the MR thermometry
approach is robust against spin order collapse and water evaporation and is
applicable to a bed material that is not optically transparent. The main
limitations of this work are the limitations to the temperature range and the
possibility to acquire less than 10 temperature maps per minute. The latter is
primarily caused by the necessity to adapt the MR imaging sequence to the
particular bed material used. Future optimization of the imaging protocol is
expected to open up the full potential of MR thermometry for the characterization
of catalytic fixed bed reactors.

new class of maps called oriented
colored broken submersions. This is the simplest class of maps that satisfies a
version of the b-principle and in dimension 2 approximates the class of
oriented submersions well in the sense that every oriented colored broken
submersion of dimension 2 to a closed simply connected manifold is bordant to a
submersion.
  We show that the Madsen-Weiss theorem (the standard Mumford Conjecture) fits
a general setting of the b-principle. Namely, a version of the b-principle for
oriented colored broken submersions together with the Harer stability theorem
and Miller-Morita theorem implies the Madsen-Weiss theorem.
  The b-principle for oriented colored broken submersions is equivalent to the
following statement: the structure set of the group of oriented colored broken
submersions to a closed simply connected manifold is bivariant with respect to
shorter maps. We show that it really is bivariant.
  The main tool here is a new class of maps called oriented colored broken
submersions which makes possible to unify two main ideas of the b-principle: a
stability-like result (as Harer stability theorem) and a class of maps which
approximates a submersion (as smooth approximations in the standard b-principle).
  In particular, a version of the b-principle for oriented colored broken
submersions to dimension 2 which approximates a submersion together with the
Harer stability theorem implies the standard Mumford Conjecture.
  We hope that a version of the b-principle for oriented colored broken
submersions to dimension 3 together with the Morita stability theorem implies
the surgery version of the standard Mumford Conjecture (which is equivalent to
the standard one by the surgery version of the Lickorish-Wall theorem).
  It would be interesting to see if there is a way to attack the Thom conjecture
using a version of the b-principle for oriented colored broken submersions.
  The note is self-contained with respect to the construction of the group of
oriented colored broken submersions and the proof of the bivariance of its
structure set. In particular, it does not rely on the Madsen-Weiss theorem.
  Experts in the construction of groups of submersions may easily extract from
the paper a general construction of such groups.

gradient masking is
amongst proposed adversarial defenses. Defenses that rely on this phenomenon
are considered failed, and can easily be broken. Despite this, new techniques
are still being developed using gradient masking, which makes it important to
understand why some approaches based on gradient masking work and others do not.
In this work, we systematically analyze the relationship between gradient
masking, the capacity of the generator, and the ability of the discriminator,
as it relates to both adversarial robustness and ability to be trained. We
illustrate our findings through both synthetic and real-world experiments.
Specifically, we demonstrate that the question of whether a particular model
based on gradient masking is a failed defense or not depends on the
transformation applied by the generator. Some transformations have the power to
relatively well-maintain the original gradient, while other transformations are
fundamentally different from the original gradient and have a very limited
ability to be learned by the discriminator. We propose a new framework for
assessing the quality of gradient masking based on the degree to which the
generator is necessary for the learning of the discriminator.
  We demonstrate that even simple models based on our framework can outperform
state of the art defenses. This suggests that the lesson learned from analyzing
failed defenses can be used to build effective defenses, answering the
otherwise open question of how to build successful gradient masking models.
Further, we demonstrate the flexibility of our work by showing that our
analysis can be extended to other transformations used for adversarial attacks.
Finally, our work provides a set of guidelines for building successful models
based on gradient masking.
  Which transformations are required to maintain the gradient for effective
learning? This question is key to building successful gradient masking models.
Previous work has demonstrated that different transformations have different
abilities to maintain the gradient, but it has not systematically analyzed
which features of the transformation are required for effective learning.
Specifically, it has not compared the success of different transformations.
We answer this question by comparing the success of different transformations
that have been used for gradient masking. We propose a framework for comparing
the success of different transformations based on the degree to which the
generator is required for the learning of the discriminator. Our analysis
demonstrates that the success of a transformation for gradient masking depends
fundamentally on the degree to which the transformation maintains the gradient
and the capacity of the generator. This work provides a set of guidelines for
building successful models based on gradient masking.

improved calibration. The idea is first to model the expected probability

asiperiodic lattices are known
to exhibit a sharp localization transition. We theoretically predict and
experimentally observe that the localization of light in one-dimensional
photonic quasicrystals may be followed by a second delocalization transition
for some states on increasing quasiperiodic modulation strength - an example of
a reentrant transition. We further propose that this phenomenon can be
qualitatively captured by a dimerized tight-binding model with long-range
couplings.
  We find that the reentrant transition is characterized by a midgap state
with a flat energy curve in the dimerized model. Its physical picture can be
captured by a effective Peierls spring attached to a moving particle. The
flat band appears when the spring becomes effectively coupled to its periodic
image. We also show that the reentrant transition is generic, affecting a
spectral range that increases with the symmetry of the lattice.
  The prediction of a moving particle attached to a effective Peierls spring
provides a simple way to engineer the delocalization of states in
quasiperiodic lattices. The localization of light is also of practical
interest, as it may be used to create optical circuits with extremely long
localization lengths. Our results further open the possibility of using
quasiperiodic lattices to study the physics of a moving band edge state.
Finally, our work contributes to the further development of the fundamental
connection between spatial symmetry of a lattice and the delocalization of its
states.
  We hope that this work inspires further fundamental investigations on
quasiperiodic lattices, tight-binding models with long-range couplings and the
physics of a moving band edge state. It also contributes to the development of
more efficient optical devices with extremely long localization lengths.

In this work, we present our results on the ARID dataset. Most previous works
only evaluate performance on large, well illuminated datasets like Kinetics and
HMDB51. We demonstrate that our work is able to achieve a very low error rate
while being trained on a much smaller dataset of dark videos. We also explore a
variety of training and inference strategies including domain transfer
methodologies and also propose a simple but useful frame selection strategy.
Our empirical results demonstrate that we beat previously published baseline
models by 11%.
  We also observe that training models on large illuminated datasets and then
applying dark frames during inference is a simple yet effective trick to
improve performance on the ARID dataset. We get a 7% error rate improvement by
using this trick.
  We also observe that simple frame selection strategies like finding the median
frame (based on pixel intensity) and evaluating the video as a movie gives
better results than evaluating the video as a collection of frames. We get a 5%
error rate improvement by using this trick.
  Finally, we also observe that training models on random clips of dark videos
gives better results than training models on full videos. We get a 4% error rate
improvement by using this trick.
  We also try different model architectures and find that ResNet-18 gives the
best results compared to R2D, BGN and I3D.
  We also try different training methodologies and find that fine tuning a
pretrained model on dark videos gives better results than end to end training.
We get a 3% error rate improvement by fine tuning models.
  We also try different inference strategies and find that evaluating a video
as a movie gives better results than evaluating a video as a sequence of frames.
We get a 2% error rate improvement by doing this.
  We also try data augmentation during training and find that it gives a small
benefit but also increases training time.
  Finally, we try batch normalization domain adaptation strategies and find that
they give a small benefit but also increase training time.

effect, where the exchange can be either strongly suppressed or enhanced,

in large-scale silicon superconducting quantum computing architectures.

used to switch a negatively exchanged pair to a positively exchanged one simply

contributes to Giudici, Li and Praeger's program for the classification of
locally arc transitive graphs by showing that the star normal quotient twisted
wreath category also contains infinitely many graphs.
  From a structural point of view, these graphs exhibit a new relationship
between the local structure and the global action of the automorphism group. A
novel technique is developed to produce this relationship and the structure of
the automorphism groups is then driven by capturing this local global link.
Specifically, we use a new version of the star normal quotient to link the
local structure to the action of the automorphism group on vertices. This
approach provides a common framework between the construction of these graphs
and the proof that they are quasiprimitive.

Specifically, given a local structure we determine the action of the automorphism
group on vertices. In contrast, the approach of Giudici, Li and Praeger to
construct these graphs starts with an action of the automorphism group on vertices
and then forces a local structure. While our method is restricted to the local
structures that we know how to use in this way, it is not clear from the work of

vast spectrum of natural language tasks. However, it is largely unexplored
whether they can better internalize knowledge from a structured data, such as a
knowledge graph, or from text. In this work, we propose a method to infuse
structured knowledge into LLMs, by directly training T5 models on factual
triples of knowledge graphs (KGs). We show that models pre-trained on Wikidata
KG with our method outperform the T5 baselines on FreebaseQA and WikiHop, as
well as the Wikidata-answerable subset of TriviaQA and NaturalQuestions. The
models pre-trained on factual triples compare competitively with the ones on
natural language sentences that contain the same knowledge. Trained on a
smaller size KG, WikiMovies, we saw 3x improvement of exact match score on
MetaQA task compared to T5 baseline. The proposed method has an advantage that
no alignment between the knowledge graph and text corpus is required in
curating training data. This makes our method particularly useful when working
with industry-scale knowledge graphs.
  We also observe that the T5 models trained on factual triples tend to avoid
common stereotypical answers and choose the correct answer with a higher
confidence. We argue that the models learn the "knowledge identity" of each
factual triple, which is the combination of three entities in a specific
relation. The learned knowledge identity helps the models to choose the
correct answer on the test cases that are similar to the training examples.
Unlike previous work using hypernyms of entities, our approach does not
introduce any external knowledge source and only relies on the triples in the
knowledge graph.
  We release our training data on Wikidata and WikiMovies, as well as the
model checkpoints, for the community to explore.
  We also achieve excellent results on answering natural questions from
multiples facts. We answer questions with two answers by ranking the top
candidates from the union of solo answers of the two entities involved in the
question and selecting the top two. Out of 407 unique questions, we get 397
(out of 397) questions correct.
  Overall, we believe that our method has the potential to utilize the
extensive structured knowledge from knowledge graphs for improving the
performance of LLMs, especially on cross-linked questions that touch multiple
entities.

regions relevant to Parkinson's Disease based on local field potential data
collected from the brain of marmoset monkeys. Parkinson's disease is a
neurodegenerative disorder, linked to the death of dopaminergic neurons at the
substantia nigra pars compacta, which affects the normal dynamics of the basal
ganglia-thalamus-cortex neuronal circuit of the brain. Although there is no
cure for this disease, a better understanding of the dynamics of the parkinsonian
circuit could lead to improvements in treatment. With that in mind, we use a
computational model to study the effect of the loss of dopamine neurons on the
normal dynamics of the basal ganglia-thalamus-cortex neuronal circuit. More
specifically, our model includes mesencephalic (nigra and substantia nigra) and
basal ganglia (caudate nucleus, putamen, globus pallidus, internal and external)
neurocircuits and we simulate the application of high and low levels of dopamine
on the system. We found that the parkinsonian circuit presents a switch in the
frequency of the oscillations from the normal system (around 6Hz to 8Hz, gamma
frequency) to the disease condition (around 2Hz, delta frequency), that can be
normalized with normal dopamine levels. This normalized frequency is now
reported to be around 4Hz. This model can now be used to test other parkinsonian
features, to test the effect of L-DOPA and to understand the effect of
neurotransmitter replacement at different basal ganglia neurons.
  We find that the replacement of dopamine in the parkinsonian system leads to
a normalization of the frequency of the Thalamus and Cortex but not in the
Basal Ganglia. This could explain some side effects of L-DOPA such as dyskinesia
that some patients present. The normalized frequency of the Thalamus and Cortex
may also be the result of other changes in the system besides the replacement of
dopamine. It is possible that the treatment of PD could lead to the
normalization of the Thalamus and Cortex oscillations at the cost of other
changes in the system. The future version of the model will need to include
other neurotransmitter systems in order to disentangle the effects of dopamine
and other neurotransmitters on the basal ganglia-thalamus-cortex

camera to predict weather conditions. These solutions have resulted in
incremental cost and limited scope. To ensure smooth operation of all
transportation services in all-weather conditions, a reliable detection system
is necessary to classify weather in wild. The challenges involved in solving
this problem is that weather conditions are diverse in nature and there is an
absence of discriminate features among various weather conditions. The existing
works to solve this problem have been scene specific and have targeted
classification of two categories of weather. In this paper, we have created a
new open source dataset consisting of images depicting three classes of weather
i.e rain, snow and fog. A novel algorithm has been designed and implemented in
order to classify the three categories of weather. The algorithm is based upon
convolutional neural networks (CNN) and has been named as RSFNet. The CNN part
of the proposed system has been designed to first classify the image as clear
and cloudy and a separate network has been trained to classify the clear and
cloudy images into one of the three categories. The proposed system has been
tested on 80000 images and has given promising results.

an approach to improving
the representation of convection in weather and climate models. This is an
attractive framework as it is fundamentally dynamical, removing some of the
assumptions of mass-flux convection schemes which are invalid at current model
resolutions. However, it is still not understood how best to close the
multi-fluid equations for atmospheric convection. In this paper we develop a
simple two-fluid, single-column model with one rising and one falling fluid. No
further modelling of sub-filter variability is included. We then apply this
model to Rayleigh-B\'{e}nard convection, showing that, with minimal closures,
the correct scaling of the heat flux (Nu) is predicted over six orders of
magnitude of buoyancy forcing (Ra). This suggests that even a very simple
two-fluid model can accurately capture the dominant coherent overturning
structures of convection.
  In a follow-up paper we extend this simple two-fluid framework to axisymmetric
simulations of idealised tropical convection. While the overall heat flux is
reasonably well predicted, the scaling of the individual fluids is not what one
would naively expect, and further work is clearly needed to confidently close
the equations for axisymmetric convection.
  We also show that, interestingly, a very similar formulation can be derived
by averaging the Euler equations with a particular class of coherent structure
representatives, namely clusters of up-downdrafts. This further justifies the
formulation of the closures in the multi-fluid framework.
  The simplicity of the closures developed here is crucial to the model's
success. Closing the model equations for convection is clearly an open problem
and further work is required to confidently resolve the sub-filter variability
in the atmosphere.

scale up these results to 3D global models. However, as a first step in
developing new convection schemes for numerical models, it is essential to
validate the simulations with rigorous laboratory experiments, such as those
possible in a large water tank. This is a more controlled environment than
idealised numerical simulations, but still captures the same physical
processes of turbulence as numerical models used in large eddy simulations.

Twitter provides organizations and
individuals an effective way to monitor public emotions towards them and their
competitors. As a result, sentiment analysis has become an important and
challenging task. In this work, we have collected seven publicly available and
manually annotated twitter sentiment datasets. We create a new training and
testing dataset from the collected datasets. We develop an LSTM model to
classify sentiment of a tweet and evaluate the model with the new dataset.
The model yields accuracy of 83% on the testing dataset.
  We perform the following experiments on the LSTM model: i) Cross-validation
experiment: We create a new training and testing dataset for every iteration of
the cross-validation experiment. ii) Dataset variability experiment: We create a
training and testing dataset for every iteration of the dataset variability
experiment. iii) Parameter variability experiment: We create a new training and
testing dataset for every iteration of the parameter variability experiment. We
make the following observations from the experiments: i) The accuracy of the
model is sensitive to the training and testing dataset. ii) The accuracy of the
model is relatively insensitive to the parameters of the model.
  We observe the following: i) The accuracy of the model on a single dataset is
low. ii) The error of the model on a single dataset is sensitive to the
distribution of the sentiment labels. iii) The sentiment labels are not
balanced in the training datasets. iv) The text preprocessing of the model is
not optimized. v) LSTM model is relatively insensitive to parameter variability
when there is plenty of training data. We suggest the following future work: i)
More care needs to be taken when creating and using sentiment annotation guides.
In particular the guide should be validated before a large scale annotation
campaign is undertaken. ii) More diverse training datasets are needed. iii) The
text preprocessing of the model should be optimized. iv) We observe that there
are only a few studies on social media sentiment analysis that look at the
impact of sentiment label imbalance. There is a need for more work on this
topic.
  We release the following: i) A Python script that creates the new training
and testing dataset from the collected datasets. ii) A Python script that
performs the cross-validation experiment. iii) A Python script that performs the
dataset variability experiment. iv) A Python script that performs the parameter
variability experiment.

treatments are often evaluated by analyzing the average treatment effects and
risks. The stochastic efficiency with respect to a function is often employed
in such evaluations through ranking the certainty equivalents of each
treatment. The main challenge of using this method is gathering an adequate
number of observations to produce results with statistical power. However, in
many cases, only a limited number of trials are replicated in field
experiments, leaving an inadequate number of observations. In addition, this
method focuses only on the farmer's profit without incorporating the impact of
disease pressure. The objective of our study is to develop a method to address
the issue of an insufficient number of observations when evaluating
pesticides. We use a mixed-effects model incorporating the number of trials as
a random effect and include disease pressure as an interacting factor. We
apply the proposed method using simulated and real data sets.
  Our results show that incorporating the number of trials as a random effect
in the model allows farmers to know which treatments are significantly
different from the others at trial and farm levels. Without this approach, the
significance of the differences is only known at the trial level in the real
data example we present.

However, such a watching experience is often hindered by the frequent
dropped frames due to the limited bandwidth. One of the major reasons for the
frame drops is the costly state synchronization after significant video
processing, e.g., skyline detection, in 360-degree video streaming. In this
paper, we propose a novel skyline synchronization (SS) protocol for 360-degree
video streaming to avoid such frame drops. In the SS protocol, the skyline
detected in each video frame is encoded with a unique signature and sent to
the receivers through the network. Based on the received skyline signatures,
each receiver can locally synchronize the skyviews and notify the sender of
their synchronization states, if necessary. Thus, the senders can insert the
missing skyviews to the streaming bitstreams to avoid the frame drops. The
SS protocol is purely decentralized, transparent, and implementation-agnostic.
Moreover, it is adaptable to various video streaming infrastructures. We
implement the SS protocol and evaluate its effectiveness in reducing frame
drops for various 360-degree video scenes. The experimental results show that
the SS protocol can reduce frame drops by up to $99.4\%$ in various
environments.

would appear at a well-known frequency $f_{\rm EP}$ depending on the

the data available prevents us from unequivocally tackling this task. We show
that glitches affect the test of the WEP, up to an a priori unknown level.

lateral nanoscale dimensions, crucial for potential device downscaling, while

anisotropy is extremely challenging. Here we integrate nanosized

anisotropy, within a gold plasmonic nanoantenna array to design
micrometer-scale a magnetophotonic crystal that exhibit abrupt and narrow
magneto-optical spectral features that are both magnetic field and light
incidence direction controlled. The narrow Fano-type resonance arises through
the interference of the individual nanoantenna's surface plasmons and a
Rayleigh anomaly of the whole nanoantenna array, in both optical and
magneto-optical spectra, which we demonstrate and explain using Maxwell-theory
simulations. This robust magnetophotonic crystal opens the way for conceptually
new high-resolution light incidence direction sensors, as well as for building
blocks for plasmon-assisted all-optical magnetization switching in

to facilitate provably improved downstream imitation learning? In this work, we
answer this question affirmatively and present training objectives that use
offline datasets to learn a factored transition model whose structure enables
the extraction of a latent action space. Our theoretical analysis shows that
the learned latent action space can boost the sample-efficiency of downstream
imitation learning, effectively reducing the need for large near-optimal expert
datasets through the use of auxiliary non-expert data. To learn the latent
action space in practice, we propose TRAIL (Transition-Reparametrized Actions

model contrastively, and uses the transition model to reparametrize the action
space for sample-efficient imitation learning. We evaluate the practicality of
our objective through experiments on a set of navigation and locomotion tasks.

we can obtain policies that achieve near-human performance using fewer than
100 suboptimal trajectories as input to our objective.

to improve the efficiency of
reinforcement learning by exploiting the expert demonstrations. However, in
many real scenarios, obtaining expert demonstrations could be extremely
expensive or even impossible. To overcome this challenge, in this paper, we
propose a novel learning framework called Co-Imitation Learning (CoIL) to
exploit the past good experiences of the agents themselves without expert
demonstration. Specifically, we train two different agents via letting each of
them alternately explore the environment and exploit the peer agent's
experience. While the experiences could be valuable or misleading, we propose
to estimate the potential utility of each piece of experience with the expected
gain of the value function. Thus the agents can selectively imitate from each
other by emphasizing the more useful experiences while filtering out noisy
ones. Experimental results on various tasks show significant superiority of the
proposed Co-Imitation Learning framework, validating that the agents can
benefit from each other without external supervision.
  We further analyze the theoretical properties of the proposed approach and
connect it to existing multi-agent reinforcement learning, as well as
bilateral constrained optimization to induce cooperative behavior if the
agents are best served by working together. Experimental results on
negotiation and cooperative games show that the proposed framework can achieve
optimal or near-optimal cooperation, while much faster than the traditional
reinforcement learning.
  In conclusion, this work presents a novel perspective of exploiting the past
experiences of the agents themselves for imitation learning without external
expert demonstration. The proposed Co-Imitation Learning framework is proven to
be effective and efficient via thorough experimental investigations, which could
also relieve the sample complexity of reinforcement learning in real scenarios.
As the agents learn from each other, the proposed approach can induce
cooperative behavior if the agents are best served by working together, which
is an added bonus of the framework.

translation (NMT) performance. However, recent work has argued that the gains
produced by RL for NMT are mostly due to promoting tokens that have already
received a fairly high probability in pre-training. We hypothesize that the
large action space is a main obstacle to RL's effectiveness in MT, and conduct
two sets of experiments that lend support to our hypothesis. First, we find
that reducing the size of the vocabulary improves RL's effectiveness. Second,
we find that effectively reducing the dimension of the action space without
changing the vocabulary also yields notable improvement as evaluated by BLEU,
semantic similarity, and human evaluation. Indeed, by initializing the
network's final fully connected layer (that maps the network's internal
dimension to the vocabulary dimension), with a layer that generalizes over
similar actions, we obtain a substantial improvement in RL performance: 1.5
BLEU points on average.

reasonable, and thus offers a promising direction for further RL research in

role of the Web as a driver of polarization. In order to further our
understanding of the factors behind online polarization, in the present work we
collect and analyze Web browsing histories of tens of thousands of users
alongside careful measurements of the time spent browsing various news sources.
We show that online news consumption follows a polarized pattern, where users'
visits to news sources aligned with their own political leaning are
substantially longer than their visits to other news sources. Next, we show
that such preferences hold at the individual as well as the population level,
as evidenced by the emergence of clear partisan communities of news sources
from aggregated browsing patterns. Finally, we tackle the important question of
the role of user choices in polarization. Are users simply following the links
proffered by their Web environment, or do they exacerbate partisan polarization
by intentionally pursuing like-minded news sources? To answer this question, we
compare browsing patterns with the underlying hyperlink structure spanned by
the considered news sources, finding strong evidence of polarization in
partisan browsing habits beyond that which can be explained by the hyperlink
structure of the Web.
  In particular, we show that the strength of polarization in the hyperlink
structure of Web pages is a small fraction (about 16%) of the strength of
polarization in the time spent on links by users. This is true even after
controlling for the fact that some links are substantially heavier than others,
as evidenced by the small variance of the normalized time spent on links
relative to the variance of the time spent on links itself). That is, while
the Web does provide hyperlinks that can be used to further polarization, the
majority of the evidence points to a role of user choices in exacerbating
polarization.
  We conclude with a discussion of our results in the context of previous
literature and the need for further work to understand the factors behind
polarization and its societal implications.

the Web Conference 2019 "Why is the Web not a platform for civil discourse?"

Edges and boundaries encode shape information, while textures manifest the
appearance of regions. Despite the success of Convolutional Neural Networks
(CNNs) in computer vision and medical image analysis applications,
predominantly only texture abstractions are learned, which often leads to
imprecise boundary delineations. In medical imaging, expert manual segmentation
often relies on organ boundaries; for example, to manually segment a liver, a
medical practitioner usually identifies edges first and subsequently fills in
the segmentation mask. Motivated by these observations, we propose a
plug-and-play module, dubbed Edge-Gated CNNs (EG-CNNs), that can be used with
existing encoder-decoder architectures to process both edge and texture
information. The EG-CNN learns to emphasize the edges in the encoder, to
predict crisp boundaries by an auxiliary edge supervision, and to fuse its
output with the original CNN output. We evaluate the effectiveness of the
EG-CNN with various mainstream CNNs on two publicly available datasets, BraTS
19 and KiTS 19 for brain tumor and kidney semantic segmentation. We demonstrate
how the addition of EG-CNN consistently improves segmentation accuracy and
generalization performance.

of local (i.e., single-node) transactions, and there is no need for an explicit
coordinating node (or "coordinating primary") in a MongoDB sharded transaction.

coordinate transactions across different nodes in a distributed database. We
identify three challenges in this area, namely the treatment of the logical
primary node, the handling of transaction conflicts, and the support for
transaction isolation. We propose and evaluate different solutions to these
challenges, and provide insights into the design of MongoDB's transaction
coordinator (which is the component responsible for implementing sharded
transactions) and the logical primary node in a sharded transaction.

performance-critical transactions, and the need for further improvement of the

Biases in the dataset can be learned by the model and degrade the
generalizability of the applications. There are studies on debiased models.
However, scientists have a hard time to evaluate the contribution of a source
of bias, e.g., the bias coming from the distribution of patient gender, as
different sources of bias look very similar when only considering the
prediction outcome. Thus, the issue of evaluating the contribution of a single
source of bias has not been addressed. This is because quantifying the
\emph{individual} contribution of a bias requires us to remove the bias while
keeping all other factors the same, which is impossible in reality. For
instance, to evaluate the contribution of the bias towards female patients,
one must find training samples with very similar characteristics to other
patients but for the gender, and then retrain a model on the new dataset.
However, it is impossible to prepare such a dataset. We propose a novel
method to quantitatively evaluate the contribution of a bias towards a group of
patients. Different from previous studies on debiased models, our method
experiments a series of models trained on datasets with successively removed
sources of bias. We use pseudo-grouping of patients based on their clinical
features to evaluate the contribution of a single source of bias. The
difference of predictions on the same group of interest before and after
removing a bias provides us the contribution of that bias. The uniqueness of
our method is that it does not require any additional data nor any changes to
the training data. We use segmentation of chest CT as an example to demonstrate
the effectiveness of our method. We also show that the debiased models
constructed by simply removing the bias do not necessarily generalize
better than our method, which provides a quantitative evaluation of the
contribution of a single source of bias.

compound Bi$_5$FeTi$_3$O$_{15}$ (BFTO) at high hydrostatic pressure conditions.
The high-pressure XRD measurements show that the unit cell volume of BFTO
decretes with an increase in hydrostatic pressure, which indicates that the
average bonding between atoms gets tighter. The magnetic measurement under
high hydrostatic pressure shows a drastic change in the magnetic behavior of
this compound. The high-pressure magnetic measurement shows a sudden change in
magnetic field dependence of magnetization near 25 kBar pressure. This sudden
change indicates a possible phase transition in magnetic order near 25 kBar
pressure. The high-pressure magnetic measurement also shows a sudden change in
magnetic transition temperature near 25 kBar pressure. This sudden change in
magnetic transition temperature indicates a possible shift of magnetic
transition temperature in high hydrostatic pressure conditions. The possible
reasons of sudden change in magnetic phase in high hydrostatic pressure
conditions are disccused.
  In conclusion, high hydrostatic pressure both electrical and magnetic
measurements are needed to investigate the behavior of any compound.
  Furthermore, the possibility of changing the functional properties of any
material by changing doping site and concentration, stacking composition and
order, and hydrostatic pressure pressure makes BFTO and materials with similar
structure a subject of interest for advanced functional material research.
Finally, the possibility of growing this material in form of thin film makes
it a viable candidate for pseudo-magnetic field controlled magnetic switch and
sensor.

start local
minimization from discrete points in a distance-oracle. While such methods are
practical for solving large-scale problems, it is not fully understood how
accurate the discrete points should be. In this work, we provide a theoretical
analysis of the benefit of using discrete points from a distance-oracle,
constructing a counter-example showing that even using points from a relatively
coarse Delaunay triangulation may drastically improve computation time. We
also provide a theoretically-grounded algorithm for choosing the optimal
discretization, dependent on the oracle query cost and available computation
budget. As a by-product, we provide an efficient point-based sub-gradient
method for shortest path problems, which may be used as a key component in a
two-stage solver.
  We show that, under mild assumptions on the subgradient computation cost and
the available computation budget, our algorithm may compute a solution with an
approximation ratio of $\mathcal{O}(1+\frac{k}{\sqrt{B}})$, where $k$ is the
number of vertices in the discrete problem and $B$ is the computation budget.
Furthermore, we show that this approximation ratio is tight. We also provide a
practical algorithm which, in our experiments, produces results consistent with
our theoretical recommendations.
  Our algorithms and analysis are tested on a set of synthetic and real-world
datasets. The results show a drastic improvement in computation time (up to 5
orders of magnitude) and a small penalty in solution quality (about 3% on the
distance).
  Finally, we study the influence of using a Delaunay triangulation as a
discretization. We show both theoretically and practically that, depending on
the dataset, using a Delaunay triangulation may be beneficial (speed-up of 2
orders of magnitude on the computation time with almost no penalty on the
approximation ratio), or not (considerably larger approximation ratio). This
suggests that local search starting from discrete points may benefit from a
carefully chosen discretization, and that a continuous optimization approach
may be more robust.
  A version of this work with a different focus, the optimal choice of a
discretization for local search, has been presented in A. Arnold and J. Lang,
"On the benefit of discretizing shortest path problems", Proc. 38th Intl.

monodromy-free Schr\"odinger operators with rational potentials. We concentrate
on a class of potentials constituted by generalized Hermite polynomials. These
polynomials defined as Wronskians of classic Hermite polynomials appear in a
number of mathematical physics problems as well as in the theory of random
matrices and 1D SUSY quantum mechanics. Being quadratic at infinity, those
potentials demonstrate localized oscillatory behavior near the origin. We
derive an explicit condition of non-singularity of the corresponding potentials
and estimate a localization range with respect to indices of polynomials and
distribution of their zeros in the complex plane. It turns out that 1D SUSY
quantum mechanics allows to construct self-adjoint Schr\"odinger operators
with rational approximations of given band structures which may be of use in
the construction of fake semiconductors or generally in any application where
control over a rational band gap is required.
  In the second part of the paper we present a sample generalized Hermite
polynomial $P_{12}$ with the index $n=12$ and a degree $2n=24$. The potential
$V(x)=P_{12}(x)^2$ is meromorphic on the complex plane with a unitary pole at
the origin. Its localized behavior around zero permits to construct a family of
non-isomorphic band graphs with a rational approximation of the Harper model
eigenenergies. We prove that for $V(x)=P_{12}(x)^2$ there is no accumulation
of discrete eigenvalues at the pole, that means no monodromy in the defining
Schr\"odinger equation.

zeros as the roots of a certain hyperelliptic curve of genus $11$. The curve
defines a spectral band graph of the self-adjoint Schr\"odinger operator which

performing the delta
hedging process of a European option. This cost is represented by an
integration formula that includes European option prices and a certain function
depending on the delta process. We first define a unit liquidity cost and then
show that the liquidity cost is a multiplication of the unit liquidity cost,
stock price, supply curve parameter, and the square of the number of options.
Using this formula, the expected liquidity cost before hedging can be
calculated much faster than when using a Monte Carlo simulation. Numerically
computed distributions of liquidity costs in special cases are also provided.
The results show that the unit liquidity cost is on average $0.0003 per option,
and the total liquidity cost is on average $12.50 for a notional option with a
stock price of $100 per unit. Firms dealing in options can use this method to
estimate the expected liquidity cost before trading, helping to determine the
feasibility of a trade. Firms can also use this method to calculate the
expected liquidity cost for other products that require delta hedging.

constitute the backbone of myriad advancements in semiconductor and additive
manufacturing, communication networks, biology and medicine, defense and
national security, and a host of other sectors over the past decades. However,
accurately and efficiently modeling CPA- and NLO-based systems is challenging
because of the multitude of coupled linear and nonlinear processes present in
these systems and the diversity of material constituents. The lack of robust,
efficient, and accurate models to simulate CPA and NLO processes constitutes
the primary bottleneck to achieving breakthrough manufacturing processes and
advanced sensing and communication technologies. A first-principles
semiconductor equation that includes pump-induced index changes is too slow to
perform a single round-trip in a CPA system. Furthermore, developing a
full-scale CPA system model that includes laser cavity dynamics, is not
feasible using direct solution methods due to the excessive computational
costs. In this paper, we develop a new sub-cycling index change model for
high-power CPA systems and combine it with a sub-cycling amplitude and phase
equation to efficiently (at a fraction of the original time) model a CPA
laser. The new model predicts experimentally observed laser characteristics
such as the formation of a hot spot on the gain medium, partial cavity
instability, and the occurrence of laser misalignment and mode-beating.
Moreover, the new model provides the input signals needed to design closed
loop systems to stabilize the laser cavity. The new model also provides the
input signals needed to investigate the influence of laser design parameters
on the laser performance. To demonstrate the model's capability, we investigate
the influence of gain medium index modifications on a CPA system. The new
model is shown to predict 3 W of peak power (and 100 nJ of pulse energy) at 1
cycle of 1.05 $\mu$m within 1 $\mu$s (i.e., 1000 iterations of the amplitude
and phase equation and 100 iterations of the index change equation), a task
which takes several hours using traditional (non-sub-cycled) models. To the
authors' knowledge, this is the first model that achieves such a prediction.
  We hope that this model will provide a framework for designing, understanding
and reproducing CPA systems, and will provide a platform for investigating
laser physics, material science, and system design.

  Word ordering, as a constrained language generation task, takes unordered
words as input and arranges them into a well-formed sentence given sentence
length and part-of-speech constraints. Existing work uses constrained decoding
to solve the task, yet the methods for generating the first word in the
sentence are diverse and there lacks a unifying solution. We hypothesize that
the success of word ordering frameworks relies on effective sentence starting
methods, and empirical study confirms our hypothesis. We report the performance
of three classes of sentence starting methods (random, deterministic, and
learning-based) on various word ordering datasets and find that even the most
naive deterministic methods outperform learning-based approaches as almost all
previous work uses learning-based sentence starting, yet our sentence augmentation
is a simple trick to improve their performance. We also report that the
performance of word ordering frameworks varies greatly among different
implementations of the same algorithm and, interestingly, the variation is
correlated to the choice of sentence starting method. Code and data are

low-density parity-check (LDPC) codes assume that the degree distributions of
the two ends of a randomly selected edge are independent. In the paper, we take
one step further and consider ensembles of LDPC codes with degree-degree
correlations. For this, we propose two methods to construct an ensemble of
degree-degree correlated LDPC codes. We then derive a system of density
evolution equations for such degree-degree correlated LDPC codes over a binary
erasure channel (BEC). By conducting extensive numerical experiments, we show
how the degree-degree correlation affects the performance of LDPC codes. Our
numerical results show that LDPC codes with negative degree-degree correlation
could improve the maximum tolerable erasure probability. Moreover, a code with
a suitable positive degree-degree correlation could have the similar performance
as the degree-degree uncorrelated code.

  Quantum key distribution (QKD) provides means for unconditional secure key
transmission between two distant parties. However, in practical
implementations, it suffers from quantum hacking due to device imperfections.
Here we propose a hybrid measurement attack, with only linear optics, in a
typical way to exploit the malfunctions of a boundary between vacuum and a
non-vacuum in the QKD channel. Our scheme can be applied to several phase
randomization QKD systems involving a homodyne detector. As the homodyne detector
is phase sensitive, the boundary malfunctions providing different average
phases in the transmitted coherent states can be exploited. Our analysis shows
that the phase homodyning attack is effective when the average phase shift of
the boundary malfunction is larger than a certain value. Moreover, we propose a
polarization homodyning attack by exploiting the boundary malfunctions providing
different probabilities of being in the non-vacuum state. This attack is
effective for any value of the average phase shift of the boundary
malfunction.

in various
disciplines of science and engineering like power systems, gene-regulatory
networks, social networks, financial networks, astronomy etc. Furthermore, in
many of these applications the underlying system is dynamical in nature and
because of the complexity of the systems involved, deriving a mathematical
model which can be used for clustering and community detection, is often
impossible. Moreover, while clustering dynamical systems, it is imperative that
the dynamical nature of the underlying system is taken into account. In this
paper, we propose a novel approach for clustering dynamical systems purely from
time-series data which inherently takes into account the dynamical evolution of
the underlying system. In particular, we define a \emph{distance/similarity}
measure between the states of the system which is a function of the influence
that the states have on each other and their persistence. Using this measure, we
propose an graph-based approach for clustering dynamical systems. Finally, we
illustrate the efficacy of our approach by clustering three different
dynamical systems, namely, a synthetic system, the gene-regulatory network of
Thale cress and the network of satellites in the solar system.
  From the above three examples, it is evident, that our approach not only
correctly clusters the nodes in each system but also brings out the
\emph{community} as well as the \emph{dynamical} characteristics of each system
to light.
  In the case of the synthetic system, we demonstrate how our approach can be
used to identify the number of communities as well as the connectivity
characteristics of the underlying system.
  For the gene-regulatory network of Thale cress, we demonstrate how our approach
can be used to identify the processes that are most likely to be active while
the network is in a particular community as well as the connections between
different communities.
  Finally, we illustrate how our approach can be used to predict potential
astronomical events such as planetary mergers and close encounters from the
network of satellites in the solar system.
  The approach presented here is general and can be used to cluster and study
the structure of any dynamical system for which streaming time-series data is
available.
  Finally, it is worth noting that all the analyses presented here have been
done purely on the basis of the connectivity and the persistence of the states
without reference to any images or any geographical location of the underlying
nodes.

planetary system to another
(interstellar panspermia) has a long history, but this hypothesis is difficult
to test through observations. We develop a mathematical model that takes
parameters such as the microbial survival lifetime, the stellar velocity
dispersion, and the dispersion of ejecta into account in order to assess the
prospects for detecting interstellar panspermia. We show that the correlations
between pairs of life-bearing planetary systems (embodied in the
pair-distribution function from statistics) may serve as an effective
diagnostic of interstellar panspermia, provided that the velocity dispersion of
ejecta is greater than the stellar dispersion. We provide heuristic estimates
of the model parameters for various astrophysical environments, and conclude
that open clusters and globular clusters appear to represent the best targets
for assessing the viability of interstellar panspermia.

then the observed trajectory of 'Oumuammu is consistent with the asteroid
carrying microorganisms derived from a planetary system separated by Gpc. We
conclude that while the evidence is tenuous, it is consistent with the hypothesis
of interstellar panspermia. Further analysis of astronomical pathways via
panspermia will require a systematic parametrization of the problem, which we
present in this work.

asteroids after leaving their parent star systems, and find that this process
is more efficient than interstellar panspermia can explain for the observed
population of isolated exoplanets. Upon subtraction of the contribution from
this process, we obtain an upper bound on the fraction of life-bearing systems
among isolated exoplanets of $2\times 10^{-5}$. We argue that this bound is
relevant to assessments of the likelihood of discovering biosignatures from
isolated exoplanets.

biosignatures which is immune to contamination from or to the influence of the
parent star system. We argue that exoplanets with orbital periods between a
few au and tens of au may be the best targets for searching for signs of life,
and that such exoplanets may be more likely to harbor life which is capable of
producing large amounts of gas which can be detected from Earth.

for understanding and
studying political polarization in political and social systems. Several
methods are used commonly to measure polarization in social networks by purely
inspecting their structure. We analyse eight of such methods and show that all
of them yield high polarization scores even for random networks with similar
density and degree distributions to typical real-world networks. Further, some
of the methods are sensitive to degree distributions and relative sizes of the
polarized groups. We propose normalization to the existing scores and a minimal
set of tests that a score should pass in order for it to be suitable for
separating polarized networks from random noise. The performance of the scores
increased by 38%-220% after normalization in a classification task of 203
networks. Further, we find that the choice of method is not as important as
normalization, after which most of the methods have better performance than the
best-performing method before normalization. This work opens up the possibility
to critically assess and compare the features and performance of different
methods for measuring structural polarization.
  We also introduce a novel framework for evaluating the effectiveness of
polarization measures. The framework treats the methods as hypotheses and
networks as experiments. Each network is labeled by an expert as either
polarized or not polarized. We test the methods using the network dataset and
report the percentage of the dataset that is correctly classified by the
methods. We also report the false positive and false negative rates of the
methods, which is not done previously in the literature.
  Further, we introduce a new network dataset of 184 political and social
networks, across 20 different domains, spanning from high-school networks to
national networks, and from friendship networks to professional or volunteer
networks. We also release a code repository with a polarization score tester,
which can be used to evaluate the performance of the methods on a network
dataset.
  In conclusion, normalization is a vital but overlooked step in measuring
structural polarization. The performance of the methods to classify networks as
polarized or not is more than twice as good after normalization. We further
introduce a novel framework for evaluating the performance of the methods and a
comprehensive network dataset.
