connections) and inter-layer connections between them. We show that these
dynamics are equivalent to those defined on the "sum" of these matrices, filled
with appropriate zeros. This is the main result of this work. In the "normal"
connection scenario, our approach is straightforward. However, in the "non
normal" connection case, a more intricate argument is needed. Moreover, from a
physical point of view, we show that some particular configurations of these
matrices lead to a decoupling of the system, such that different subsets of the
network evolve as independent modules. Moreover, in some cases, these modules
reach a synchronized state.

development, testing, and evolution. Our geometric theory of testing is
intended to serve as the specification of a testing environment, included as
the last stage of a program under test. The testing environment, implementing
our specification, drives the program under test to the desired states and
terminates it in the desired conditions. The test results include information
about the correctness of the program under test and time needed to conduct the
test. Our testing framework is general, applicable to programs developed in
any language, and applicable to programs of any type, except those involving

requirements.
  Given a set $S$ representing states, a set $A$ representing actions, and
two sets $E \subseteq S \times A \times S$ and $F \subseteq S \times A \times
S$ for expected and observed transitions, a test is constructed to lead the
program being tested to a state $q_i \in S$ and to terminate only after the
program repeats all of the transitions specified by the test path leading to
$q_i$. A path is a sequence of states starting at an initial state $s_0 \in
S$ and ending at $q_i$. A test is a set of all paths leading to a test case.
A test case is a path plus a termination condition. A termination condition
specifies the reason for terminating the test, whether due to an error in the
program, or a limit on the time available to conduct the test, or both. The
test results are then sent to the test administrator as an output of the
testing program. The test results include all of the transitions of the test
path which are due to actions of the testing program, all of which are
correctly leading the program under test to the desired state, plus any
unusual conditions such as excessive time needed to conduct the test or parts
of the test which must be terminated prematurely because of an error in the
program under test.

generate hyper-prompts: we propose HyperPrompt, a novel architecture for
prompt-based task-conditioning of self-attention in Transformers. The
hyper-prompts are end-to-end learnable via generation by a HyperNetwork.
HyperPrompt allows the network to learn task-specific feature maps where the
hyper-prompts serve as task global memories for the queries to attend to, at
the same time enabling flexible information sharing among tasks. We show that
HyperPrompt is competitive against strong multi-task learning baselines with as
few as $0.14\%$ of additional task-conditioning parameters, achieving great
parameter and computational efficiency. Through extensive empirical
experiments, we demonstrate that HyperPrompt can achieve superior performances
over strong T5 multi-task learning baselines and parameter-efficient adapter
variants including Prompt-Tuning and HyperFormer++ on Natural Language
Understanding benchmarks of GLUE and SuperGLUE across many model sizes.

perform significantly better when fine-tuned alone than a separately learned
prompt. We also propose few-shot task conditioning evaluation settings and

estimate of $\log(n)$ with high probability; the correct estimate of the
network size will be known to a large fraction ($(1 - \epsilon)$-fraction, for

rounds, and requires only random access to an implicit, a.k.a. "black-box",

size in a semi-synchronous system with Byzantine nodes; our work builds on the
ideas of these two previous works and generalizes the analysis to the full
information model, which is more difficult to analyze.

vanishing magnetization has renewed interest in understanding and engineering

classes that exhibit a variety of interesting properties owing to a complex
electronic band structure and magnetic ordering. Reports on the anomalous

reliably quantifying the anomalous Nernst coefficient. Here, we report
experiments on the anomalous Nernst effect in antiferromagnetic antiperovskite
Mn$_3$NiN thin films. Measurement of both the anomalous Hall and Nernst effects
using the same sample and measurement geometry makes it possible to directly
compare these two effects and quantify the anomalous Nernst coefficient and
conductivity in Mn$_3$NiN. We carefully evaluate the spatial distribution of
the thermal gradient in the sample and use finite element modeling to
corroborate our experimental results.
  The anomalous Nernst coefficient and conductivity are found to be
respectively $\theta_{0,N} = -107$ K/Oe and $\mathcal{N} = 0.22$ Ocm/K. Being one
of the largest reported values, the anomalous Nernst coefficient in Mn$_3$NiN,
and possibly other antiferromagnetic antiperovskites, makes rapid evaluation of
thermal emf in magnetic antiferromagnets a viable option for further
investigation. Further, we demonstrate that the anomalous Nernst coefficient
can be used as a tool to evaluate the spin Hall angle of the sample.
Specifically, using the measured anomalous Nernst coefficient and conductivity,
we find that it directly evaluates the spin Hall angle in Mn$_3$NiN with
$\theta_{SH} = \mathcal{N} \theta_{N0}/\mathcal{R} = 0.29$ mu$_B$/Oe, where
$\mathcal{R}$ is the resistivity in the longitudinal configuration.
Experiments on the spin Hall effect in Mn$_3$NiN give a similar value of
$\theta_{SH}$. The agreement between these two independent methods gives high
confidence in our results and demonstrates the utility of the anomalous Nernst
effect in evaluating the spin Hall angle in magnetic materials.

  In the first part of the lecture the basic concepts of transverse and
longitudinal beam dynamics will be introduced. The focus will be on the
differential equations describing the beam motion in the transverse and
longitudinal planes, on the most relevant beam dynamics issues in a circular
machine (closed orbit, beta and tune motion) and on the components of a
particle beam feedback system.
  In the second part of the lecture the most relevant beam loss mechanisms in
a circular machine (instability losses, residual alignment errors, electrical
discharges, incremental conductance losses, raster effects, mechanical losses
and protuberance losses) will be presented and discussed.
  The lecture will be followed by an interactive session where the students
will have the opportunity to practice their knowledge by solving problems and
investigating beam dynamics phenomena with the help of a beam dynamics
simulation program.

  We propose a novel model-parallel learning method, called local critic training
for training neural networks through error gradients estimated by additional
modules called local critic networks. We show that the proposed approach successfully
decouples the update process of layer groups for both CNNs and RNNs. We
demonstrate that the proposed method is guaranteed to converge to a critical
point and prove a technique to achieve minimum loss function value. We also
show that trained networks by the proposed method can be used for structural
optimization. Experimental results show that our method achieves satisfactory
performance, reduces training time greatly, and decreases memory consumption
per machine.
  Model parallelism is a promising approach to train large neural networks by
dividing them into smaller parts and execute these parts on different GPUs or
TPUs. However, the partitioning process is not trivial since the computation
flow among the network parts needs to be preserved for correct computation.
Although some algorithms have been proposed to automatically partition networks
for model parallelism, they are still not generic enough to handle all types
of networks. In this paper, we present a generic framework for automatic
network partitioning for model parallelism, called Graph Partitioning Network
(GPN). We represent a network as a computational graph, and partition the
computational graph for model parallelism using graph partitioning techniques.
We implement the proposed framework and achieve successful parallelization for
a variety of networks, including transformation networks for image
super-resolution, storm surge simulation networks for environmental science,
dialogue generation networks for natural language processing, and
transformer networks for natural language understanding and machine translation.

immense potential to improve the safety of high-risk engineering structures.
These materials are intrinsically self-sensing because their electrical
conductivity is affected by deformations and damage. This property, known as
piezoresistivity, has been extensively leveraged for conductivity-based damage
detection via electrical resistance change methods and tomographic imaging
techniques such as electrical impedance tomography (EIT). Although these
techniques are very effective at detecting the presence of damage, they are
limited in their ability to provide detailed information about damage shape,
size, and orientation. Such information is needed to quantify damage severity
and provide precursor indicators to failure. To this end, a novel algorithm for
imaging damage in self-sensing composites via EIT is herein presented. A
physics-based forward model that accounts for the piezoresistivity of the material
and a regularized inverse solver utilizing Morozov's discrepancy principle and
L-curve criterion are utilized in the algorithm. While these components are
well-established in the EIT literature, they are not commonly used in conjunction
with each other for distance-based regularization, and they result in highly
resolved images for a realistically modeled (i.e. inclusion of noise in the
measurements) concrete damage scenario. The result is a high-resolution image
of the damage with a degree of detail that has not been previously achieved for
a tomographic reconstruction of a large-scale, real-world engineering material
sample. Further, the algorithm is shown to be computationally efficient,
with the inverse solver being the majority of the computational time requirement
and a variety of speeding-up techniques being available. Finally, the algorithm
is validated against finite element simulations and against EIT reconstructions
obtained using a well-established but non-physically-based inverse solver.
Overall, the high-quality images obtained from the algorithm make it a promising
tool for in-situ damage imaging in real-world self-sensing composite structures.

piezoresistivity of the material is shown to be important for obtaining high-resolution
images, and thus such a model is in high demand for EIT algorithms for

physics course, with a focus on the heterogeneous impact of remote learning.
Heterogeneity is measured by comparing students who took the course before the
pandemic to students who took the course during the pandemic, while controlling
for student demographics and academic background. I find that students who
learned remotely during the pandemic scored 7% lower on a conceptual multiple
choice exam than students who learned in-person before the pandemic, and that
this deficit translates to about one letter grade. Further investigation
reveals that remote learning increased the variance of students' learning
outcomes, and that some students performed better under remote conditions while
others performed much worse. I also find that the learning loss due to remote
learning is primarily due to the lack of face-to-face instruction time rather
than the lack of face-to-face office hours time. Finally, I also find that the
learning loss due to remote learning is greater for students who are more
technologically anxious. My findings have important implications for how to
deliver instruction in a way that minimizes the loss of face-to-face time
needed to keep up with the pace of instruction.
  This work is a response to the COVID-19 pandemic's disruption of face-to-face
education, whose long-term consequences are yet unknown. My research contributes
to the literature by experimenting on a course that was delivered both in-person
and remotely, and measuring student outcomes in a way that controls for
selection into remote versus in-person learning. Further, my data set has
variables recording both sides of the education technology (edtech) equation:
what edtech tools are used and at what cost? Future work may investigate the
relative effectiveness of specific edtech tools, while also controlling for the
setting of those interactions.

conformal field theory that enjoy an higher-spin extension of its symmetry.
In this paper we study the free energy of Toda conformal field theories as a
function of an additional variable $\Delta$ which is conformally invariant under
the full (extended) symmetry algebra. We put forward a very general formula
for its first derivative as a sum of simple residues. We provide an
interpretation of each term in the language of Mellin transforms and conformal
blocks. This allows us to identify a series of terms which contribute to the
derivative of the free energy of a class of "cusp" four-point correlators in
Liouville and Toda theories. We give a closed form expression to each term and
use it to test the integrability of Toda conformal field theories for a
generating family of quadratics of the Casimir operators.
  We also study the structure of conformal blocks in $g<1$ Toda theories and
provide a natural generalization of the Liouville "thickness" to all conserved
charges. These "thicknesses" are used to break up the conformal block into a
series of simpler objects, each made out of products of quartic "diagonal"
operators and quartic "off-diagonal" operators, acting on the same
$\mathbb{C}^{n-1}$ and synthesizing the action of the Casimir operators.
Finally, for the benefit of the reader, we include a detailed review of the
Mellin transform approach to conformal blocks in Toda theories.
  We build upon the insights gained in this work to study four-point correlators
in Toda conformal field theories and provide a generating function which
captures all the results obtained through the residue method.

  Nested Sampling is typically used to compute the evidence, or partition
function, of a model, but that is a sum of entropies of microstates. To evaluate
the entropy of a probability distribution sampled according to a weighting
function, I use an approximation: I divide the total evidence by the average
likelihood. This is an unbiased estimator, but with a variance that is large
for small sample sizes. I recommend using more samples than I do in the
examples, and/or a smaller step size. I do not attempt to prove that my
approximation is convergent to the true entropy in general cases, only that it
works in the examples I have tried it on.

networks (GNNs) have been successfully used to learn data representations and
structures to solve classification and link prediction problems. The
applications of such methods are vast and diverse, but most of the current work
relies on the assumption of a static graph. This assumption does not hold for
many highly dynamic systems, where the underlying connectivity structure is
non-stationary and is mostly unknown. Using a static model in these
situations may result in sub-optimal performance. In contrast, modeling changes
in graph structure with time may provide a superior model of the system and
improve predictions. To this end, we propose TimeGraphNeuron (TGN), a model that
learns to represent temporal graph data. TGN combines the connectivity of the
graph with temporal information from multivariate time-series to achieve
high-performance classification and link prediction. As shown in our work,
TGN significantly outperforms static graph models as well as other temporal
connectivity features on both artificial and real datasets.
  We study TGN in a classification setup and propose a novel evaluation metric
called the "change score" to evaluate models that are fed information about
past connections in a changing system. We show that the change score can
effectively measure performance on systems with highly changing underlying
connectivity structures. Finally, we do an ablation study to examine the
importance of graph representations in TGN and investigate different learning
strategies and models that can be employed to fit real datasets.

important tools in evolutionary analysis, especially in phylogeny
reconstruction where they can be utilized for validation or serve as priors for
Bayesian methods. However, as more network generators are developed, there is a
lack of discussion or comparison for different generators. To bridge this gap,
we compare a set of phylogenetic network generators by profiling topological
summary statistics of the generated networks over the number of reticulations
and comparing the topological profiles.
  We consider 9 generators that produce networks with 1 to 7 reticulations,
define 14 topological statistics amenable to analysis, and use dimension
reduction to facilitate comparison. Our analysis reveals that some generators
produce networks with similar topological profiles, thus can be modeled with a
lower number of parameters, while others produce networks with very different
topological profiles and cannot be captured by a simple model.

processes that different generators model and the parameters that they need to

biodiversity contributes to the great locomotory design and mode diversity.
Various creatures make use of legs, wings, fins and other means to move through
the world. In this report, we refer to the locomotion of general biological
species as biolocomotion. We present a computational approach to detect
biolocomotion in unprocessed video.
  Significantly, the motion exhibited by the body parts of a biological entity
to navigate through an environment can be modeled by a combination of an
overall positional advance with an overlaid asymmetric oscillatory pattern, a
distinctive signature that tends to be absent in non-biological objects in
locomotion. We exploit this key trait of positional advance with asymmetric
oscillation along with differences in an object's common motion (extrinsic
motion) and localized motion of its parts (intrinsic motion) to detect
biolocomotion. An algorithm is developed to measure the presence of these
traits in tracked objects to determine if they correspond to a biological
entity in locomotion. An alternative algorithm, based on generic features
combined with learning is assembled out of components from allied areas of
investigation, also is presented as a basis of comparison.
  A novel biolocomotion dataset encompassing a wide range of moving biological
entities is assembled and released to support the proposed work. A carefully
designed experiment to evaluate the proposed approach is conducted on the
available public video datasets, in addition to the new biolocomotion dataset.
The results of the experiment show that the proposed approach outperforms the
learning approach but significantly falls short in scenes with non-biological
loocomotion, likely due to over specialization. The report concludes with a
discussion of the results, and directions for future work.

permission-less public blockchain platforms attractive for adoption as

cybercriminals to exploit vulnerabilities in blockchain platforms and target
users with social engineering attacks. Phishing is one of the most common types
of attacks that target victims with malicious intents. Due to the limited
capacity of cryptocurrency transactions, phishing attacks often target for
vulnerable victims to trick them into sending traditional (faster and larger
value) payments with the stolen cryptocurrencies. This paper proposes a
methodology to detect phishing attacks on cryptocurrency users. The proposed
methodology leverages machine learning (ML) with natural language processing
(NLP) to classify phishing URLs as legitimate or phishing. This is the first
known attempt to classify cryptocurrency phishing URLs using ML and NLP in the
literature. We have created a unique dataset of 2210 cryptocurrency phishing
URLs after thorough research and data cleaning. We have trained several ML
models, including the popular LSTM model with NLP, to classify the phishing
urls. The results show that the LSTM model with NLP outperforms other ML
approaches with an impressive accuracy of 91.8%. The results also show that
the proposed methodology has a very low false-positive rate of 1.4%. The
resulting model has been deployed as a web service that can classify
cryptocurrency URLs in real-time. We believe that the proposed web service can
be a practical tool to help prevent cryptocurrency phishing attacks.

background of the blockchain, cryptocurrency, phishing, ML, and NLP. Section
III reviews the related work of detecting phishing URLs. Section IV describes
the proposed methodology of detecting cryptocurrency phishing URLs. Section V
explains the data collection and data preprocessing. Section VI describes the
feature engineering and the training of the ML models. Section VII discusses
and analyzes the results. Section VIII presents the web service deployed from
the trained model. Section IX concludes the report and offers future work.

  We show that a system of two independently driven and damped harmonic
oscillators may be used to achieve an enhancement of the measurement precision
(achieving the standard limit of quantum measurement precision) of a shared
phase. Specifically, an eightfold improvement is possible if the damping
parameter is small enough. This is an unusual feature of this system, which
otherwise behaves classically. Furthermore, our analysis reveals that an
enhancement is also possible when the damping is large, provided the drivers
are intense enough. In such cases, however, the quantum origin of the
enhancement is not immediately apparent and a quantum explanation is needed.
We present a treatment that reveals that the enhancement is due to the
formation of an effective entanglement between the oscillators, which can be
explained by an entanglement oscillator metric. The success of the proposed
setup is revealed by comparing with a classical system, which shows no
enhancement. Additionally, our results are relevant for the improvement of
gravitational wave detection and the measurement of optical phases in
interstellar molecules.

deployment of HPC workloads on the best-fitting hardware. However, although
cloud and on-premise HPC systems offer similar computational resources, their
network architecture and performance may differ significantly. For example,
these systems use fundamentally different network transport and routing
protocols, which may introduce network noise that can eventually limit the
application scaling. This work analyzes network performance, scalability, and
cost of running HPC workloads on cloud systems. First, we consider latency,
bandwidth, and collective communication patterns in detailed small-scale
measurements, and then we simulate network performance at a larger scale. We
validate our approach on four popular cloud providers and three on-premise HPC
systems, showing that network (and also OS) noise can significantly impact
performance and cost both at small and large scale.
  We find that cloud networks tend to have lower bandwidth, higher latency,
and lower (but less consistent) message rates compared to on-premise HPC systems
while also offering lower cost per unit of resource. To help researchers and
system developers, we release a performance simulation framework that can be
used to evaluate the performance of different cloud providers and workload
configurations.
  By understanding the network performance of cloud systems, we can improve the
performance of running HPC workloads on clouds, and by understanding the
scalability, we can make informed deployment decisions to achieve the best
performance while controlling costs. Finally, our approach can be extended to
evaluate the performance of other services offering HPC capabilities.

learning to act in a varying context while taking into account the tradeoff
between exploration and exploitation. Despite its simplicity, the contextual
linear bandit model has proven itself to be a relevant benchmark for evaluating
the performance of reinforcement learning algorithms, and also has direct
applications in the real world (e.g. personalized news recommendations). A key
assumption in the contextual linear bandit setting, however, is that the context
takes on a finite number of possible values. In this work, we take a step
towards making the contextual linear bandit model more relevant by allowing the
context to be any context taking from a context distribution with support on an
infinite interval. That is, the context can now take on any real value and the
number of contexts encountered grows with the number of samples. We provide a
new efficient algorithm for this setting which achieves a regret bound of
$\tilde{O}(k^{2/3} d^{1/3} S^{1/3} \log(T))$, where is the number of arms $k$, the
dimension of the context $d$, the number of contexts encountered $S$, and the
number of time steps $T$. This significantly improves over the previously best
known bound of $\tilde{O}(k d S \log(T))$ established by Auer et al. (2002).
Additionally, our algorithm uses only $\tilde{O}(k | \log(T)| + d | \log(S)|)$
samples per round, improving over the per-round sample complexity of previous
works.

optimal over binary power control as $\Theta\left(\sqrt{K}\right)$ for all $K$.

I generate resistive force theory (RFT) based models of the ground reaction

learning uses the DEM simulation for training. A main observation is that the
RL policy tends to push the foot on the ground with higher force than the
RFT-based controller needs to achieve the desired height. Another observation
is that the RL policy oscillates with a frequency of 2Hz, which is likely the
double of the typical frequency of the monopod hopper. It indicates the
learning policy is able to exploit the dynamics of the monopod hopper. It is
interesting to see if we can leverage the learned pushing force pattern to the

performing model on CONDAQA (UnifiedQA-v2-3b) achieves only 42% on our
consistency metric, well below human performance which is 81%. We release our
dataset, along with fully-finetuned, few-shot, and zero-shot evaluations, to
facilitate the development of future NLP methods that work on negated language.

quantum system: Annealing explores equilibrium phases of a Hamiltonian with
slowly changing parameters and can be exploited as a tool for solving complex
optimization problems. In contrast, quenches are sudden changes of the
Hamiltonian, producing a non-equilibrium situation. Here, we investigate the
relation between the two cases. Specifically, we show that the minimum of the
annealing gap, which is an important bottleneck of quantum annealing
algorithms, can be revealed from a dynamical quench parameter which describes
the dynamical quantum state after the quench. Combined with statistical tools
including the training of a neural network, the relation between quench and
annealing dynamics can be exploited to reproduce the full functional behavior
of the annealing gap from the quench data. We show that the partial or full
knowledge about the annealing gap which can be gained in this way can be used
to design optimized quantum annealing protocols with a practical
time-to-solution benefit. Our results are obtained from simulating random Ising
Hamiltonians, representing hard-to-solve instances of the exact cover problem.
The obtained protocols are generic in the sense that they can be adapted to
other problem instances and Hamiltonians. Furthermore, we show that the
knowledge about the dynamical quench parameter can be used to improve
reversibility of the annealing process, that is, to distinguish situations in
which an annealing trial is successful (hits the ground state) from those in
which it is not.
  From a theoretical perspective, the presented approach to relate annealing
and quench dynamics offers a new connection between non-equilibrium and
equilibrium physics. It would be interesting to see if such a connection can
be exploited in other contexts as well.
  We have implemented our method in a Python package called dy Dynamics, which
is available at GitHub [1] and will be published on PyPI soon. The package
includes classes to easily simulate the time evolution of large-scale quantum
systems both for quench and annealing trials. Dy Dynamics features a
high-performance matrix exponential implementation via the
CMSolver [2]/Hipparcus [3] interface and NumPy/SciPy. You can also train a
Neural Network (NN) via Keras to classify quench data and evaluate the
annealing gap. A detailed user guide is available in the documentation [4] and

process executions, i.e., traces, compared to reference process models.
Alignments, however, assume complete process executions covering the entire

defines infix/postfix alignments, proposes approaches to their computation, and
evaluates them using real-life event data.
  We find that the proposed approaches are feasible for real-life event data,
provide sound and complete results, and come with efficient implementations.
Our analyses show that suffix alignments are computationally more expensive
than prefix alignments, but also yield higher detection quality. We
investigate the impact of alignment parameters on the detection quality and
 propose optimization strategies. Finally, we propose a technique to reduce the
number of alignments that need to be computed and provide a simple method for
detected deviation localization.
  Prefix, infix, and postfix checking are promising techniques for detecting
deviations in process executions and can benefit conformance checking,
monitoring, and process improvement. We believe that detecting complete
deviations is only the beginning and that infix/postfix checking can be
extended to partially complete deviations to further improve process quality.
Further research is needed to explore optimization techniques, define
approaches for detecting partially completed processes, and investigate how
to integrate process modeling, event data analysis, and improvement planning.

benefit from the strengths of prefix, infix, and postfix alignments.

general and can be applied to description of SA motion of solitons in any

long history in mathematics, going back to Bachet and Lagrange. While for some

known methods for decomposing an element into a sum of squares, in general, for

arbitrary global field (either a number field or a global function field) into
a sum of squares of minimal length.

symbol. First, we compute a genus symbol of the given element. Then, using
Lagrange's theorem, we construct a specific quadratic form which equals the
given element in the genus field. Finally, we prove that this quadratic form
admits an extension to the ring of integers (or the genus field) and its value
on the principal ideal (which generates the given element) is a sum of squares.

new approach to traditional
spectroscopy where the spectral cross-correlation with a template spectrum can
be done entirely on-device. By creating photonic devices with a carefully
designed, modulated transmission spectrum, the cross-correlation can be carried
out optically without requiring any dispersion, vastly simplifying the
instrument and reducing its cost. The measured correlation lag can be used for
detecting atomic/molecular species within and determining the radial velocity
of a particular astrophysical object.
  We present an overview of two design approaches that are currently being
developed that use different photonic platforms: silicon and fibre-based
photonics. The silicon photonic approach utilizes ring resonators that can be
thermo-optically modulated to carry out the cross-correlation. The fibre
approach uses customized fibre Bragg gratings (FBGs) with transmission spectra
that can be strain-modulated. Both approaches have been able to detect
molecular gas in a lab setting, and we are now in the process of on-sky
testing.
  Lastly, we discuss the future for these types of devices as their simplicity
opens up the possibility of developing low-cost, purpose-built spectrographs
for different astrophysical applications.

(PS) that wishes to learn a
model that fits data distributed on the nodes of a graph. We focus on Federated
Learning (FL) as a canonical application. One of the main challenges of FL is
the communication bottleneck between the nodes and the parameter server. A
popular solution in the literature is to allow each node to do several local
updates on the model in each iteration before sending it back to the PS. While
this mitigates the communication bottleneck, the statistical heterogeneity of
the data owned by the different nodes has proven to delay convergence and bias
the model. In this work, we study random walk (RW) learning algorithms for
tackling the communication and data heterogeneity problems. The main idea is to
leverage available direct connections among the nodes themselves, which are
typically "cheaper" than the communication to the PS. In a RW learning
algorithm, the nodes collectively move the model in the random walk at each
iteration. We provide a comprehensive theoretical analysis of convergence of
RW learning algorithms, which to the best of our knowledge is missing from the
literature. We also provide a unified framework for training over heterogeneous
data and minimizing communication bandwidth, that incorporates random walk
learning algorithms. We provide rigorous evidence that random walk learning
accelerates convergence and yields a more accurate model than standard FL. We
also provide a practical algorithm that predicts the number of local iterations
and the step size of the RW, and evaluate its effectiveness in real FL
settings.

vortices that are invariant along the rotation axis and undergo inverse
cascade. Yet, it has recently been shown to sustain fully three-dimensional
states with a downscale energy cascade. In this letter, we investigate the
statistical properties of three-dimensional rotating turbulence by the means of
direct numerical simulations in a triply periodic box where geostrophic
vortices are specifically damped. The resulting turbulent flow is an inertial
wave turbulence that verifies the Zakharov-Kolmogorov spectrum derived
analytically by Galtier (Phys. Rev. E, 68, 2003), thus offering numerical proof
of the relevance of wave turbulence theory for three-dimensional, anisotropic
waves. Lastly, we show that the same forcing leads to either geostrophic or
wave turbulence depending on the initial condition. Our results thus bring
further evidence for bi-stability in rotating turbulent flows.
  A key question in the theory of rotating turbulence is to know whether the
inertial range is bi- or uni-stable. Unstable states would mean that small
perturbations would drive the flow towards two distinct and persistent regimes
whichever initial conditions it starts with. Bi-stability would imply a
re-entrance scenario, wherein the flow may start in one of the states but end
in another one. In Godek et al. (J. Fluid Mech., 828, 2019), wave turbulence was
produced by tripping the rotation off a nearly geostrophic state. In the
opposite way, we now force the flow towards the wave turbulence state and follow
the evolution as the rotation is ramped down towards zero.
  The effect of magnetic tension on magnetohydrodynamic turbulence is not fully
understood. It has been suggested both to have a strengthening and to have a
weakening effect on the cascades, depending on the ratio of magnetic to fluid
conductivity. Here we explain the difference in findings by the fact that the
ratio of magnetic to fluid conductivity is proportional to the magnetic Prandtl
number times the Reynolds number. We thus propose a classification of the
turbulence regimes based on the magnetic Prandtl number and the Reynolds number.
  Recent numerical simulations of rapidly rotating turbulence (RT) have
considerably advanced our understanding of this problem. However, there is still
no consensus on the statistical properties of the rotationally dominated
inertial range.

criminal justice system. Using North Carolina court cases from 1994 to 2009, I
evaluate whether mental health treatment as a term of probation decreases the
likelihood that offenders return to the criminal justice system in the future.
Among offenders sentenced to probation, I compare those who were required to
seek mental health treatment to those who were not, using random variation in
judge assignment. I find that being assigned to seek mental health treatment
decreases the likelihood of three-year recidivism by 5.6 percentage points, or
17 percent. Treatment is most effective in reducing future violent and property
crimes, and the effect increases over time since conviction. A simple cost
benefit analysis suggests that the treatment-induced decrease in future crime
would be more than sufficient to offset the costs of providing treatment.
Receiving a mental health diagnosis does not appear to be necessary for treatment
to be effective. Finally, I explore mechanisms for this effect and find that
treatment is associated with increased self-reported mental health symptom
severity and mental health service use in the year following conviction, but
little change in employment or income.
  I also provide evidence on the factors that influence whether offenders are
assigned mental health treatment as a condition of probation. Judges are more
likely to assign treatment when the offender has a prior mental health disorder,
has committed a violent crime, or has excellent pre-sentence recommendations.
Assigning treatment in these cases is not associated with lower recidivism
rates, suggesting that judges may be using treatment as a way to signal that
they are taking an offender's mental health disorder seriously. I also find that
offenders who are assigned treatment have similar demographic characteristics
to those who are not assigned treatment, despite the criteria listed in the
sentencing guidelines that should prioritize treatment for offenders with
greater need.
  Finally, I explore the relationship between mental health treatment and
incarceration, using both judge assignment and self-initiated treatment as
instruments. I find that being assigned to seek mental health treatment
decreases the likelihood of being incarcerated in the future by 7.3 percentage
points, or 23 percent. Being assigned treatment is also associated with lower
average lengths of future incarceration spells.
  In conclusion, mental health treatment as a condition of probation appears to
decrease the likelihood of future crime and incarceration. Further research
should explore the mechanisms by which treatment reduces crime, and how to
increase the widespread use of treatment as a condition of probation

image segmentation tasks. In this paper, we introduce a novel regularization
strategy involving interpolation-based mixing for semi-supervised medical
image segmentation. The proposed method is a new consistency regularization
strategy that encourages segmentation of interpolation of two unlabelled
images to be consistent with the interpolation of their segmentation maps.
This is achieved by using the segmentation map as a feature instead of the
label in consistency regularization. The proposed method is also an example of
model-specific regularization that utilizes the advantage of model-specific
consistency regularization while addressing the scarcity of pixel-level
annotation. Our approach is model-agnostic and can be added to any model for
semi-supervised medical image segmentation. Experimental results on two
publicly available datasets show that the proposed method achieves better
results than existing regularization strategies.

overfitting of boundary masks, leading to the production of smoother
segmentation boundaries. This is particularly important in the medical image

macroscopic analog for studying material failure. The time scales in this
system allow both particle-relaxation dynamics and rift formation to be
resolved. In our experiments, a raft, an aggregate of particles, is stretched
uniaxially by the expansion of the air-liquid interface on which it floats. Its
failure morphology changes continuously with pulling velocity. This can be
understood as a competition between two velocity scales: the speed of
re-aggregation, in which particles relax towards a low-energy configuration
determined by viscous and capillary forces, and the difference of velocity
between neighboring particles caused by the expanding fluid. This competition
selects the cluster length, i.e., the distance between adjacent rifts. A model
based on this competition is consistent with the experimental failure patterns.
Furthermore, it predicts that the cluster length is proportional to the square of
the particle size, as we observe.
  We show that the model can also be viewed as a type of stick-break process,
popular for describing tree branchings and fractal formation. This analogy
allows us to connect the cluster length to the relaxation dynamics of particles
and to derive the scaling of the rift density from the velocity competition.
Moreover, it enables us to systematically explore the bifurcation of rifts in
the rift density versus pulling velocity diagram by considering the dynamics of
particles at the rift edges. This is in contrast to the bare stick-break
process which only accounts for mergers. The presence of branches in the rift
density versus velocity diagram is a signature of a non-equilibrium self-organized
cluster formation.

parameters -- $n$, the number of inputs, and $d$, the depth.
  This model received little attention so far. Among its motivations is the
idea to sort large data that fit into a unit of memory cost $O(1)$, where each
unit can be used for many operations. Such a unit could be implemented using
fewer than $n$ inputs (say, $k$ inputs) using the network we propose in this
paper, at the cost of an extra $O(n/k)$ units (in terms of both time and
space). Another motivation is to understand the power and necessary limitations
of sorting networks with degree $d$, a parameter of immense importance in
network theory.
  Our main result is to show a sharp boundary for the degree (depth) of such
networks: there exists a constant $c > 0$ such that any network constructed by
comparators of arity $k=O(\log n)$ must have degree at least $d = \lceil
\frac{n}{k}\rceil+1+c\log n$. This lower bound is for simple networks which
are transitive (i.e., if the output of one comparator is in, then so are its
inputs). It is easy to construct networks of degree $d-1$ for $k=n$. The
difficulty is to construct such a network when $k=n/2$. The lower bound
mentioned above is constructed for $k=n/2$, and we believe it to be sharp for
this range of $k$.

based on a new technique which counts the number of comparisons in a network,

inequality between the number of comparisons in the network and the number of
inputs it can sort, which in turn gives the lower bound for the degree of the
network.

may be useful in other arguments which try to lower bound the degree of a

a substantial impact on the production of the merger remnant. Whilst magnetic
fields do not strongly affect global properties, such as the star formation
history, they are able to influence structural properties. Specifically, we
find that MHD simulations tend to produce more disk-like remnants, whilst
hydrodynamic simulations yield elliptical remnants. This is because magnetic
fields are able to promote gas accretion and merger-driven disk formation by
providing an additional pressure term and enabling more efficient angular
momentum transport. We support this with dedicated dwarf-galaxy collision
simulations. Furthermore, we find that the inclusion of magnetic fields is able
to lead to the formation of a central black hole in one out of five merger
remnants. Finally, we find that the inclusion of magnetic fields is able to
result in the formation of magnetic fields in the merger remnant, with values
ranging from a few $\mu$G to over 20 $\mu$G. The proper treatment of
magnetic fields is able to influence structural properties of the merger
remnants in a way that is yet to be fully understood; we suggest further
investigations with sophisticated magnetized models of the interstellar medium
and including the effects of stellar feedback.

original CT slices, which will be incorporated into the input as complementary
information along with the lung lesion mask and the lung mask. The lesion
masking operation in the feature extraction network allows the model to focus
on the area affected by the infection when extracting image feature, which is
more relevant to the severity grading task, thus improving the model's ability
to distinguish severe and mild images.
  To improve the performance of the classification network, we propose a
Contrastive Mixup strategy. The Mixup is a popular ensemble method which
produces new training images by averaging two random images and their labels.
However, it only works on the image input level, whereas the COVID-19 severity
grading task is closely related to the texture pattern of the CT images,
which are not well mixed by the average operation. For example, the average CT
image may lose the lesion area, which is very important for the severity
grading task. Therefore, we further improve the Contrastive Mixup by adding
two additional contrastive learning levels on the density level and the
infection level, which effectively improves the performance.

weighted cross-entropy loss function. The loss function uses the class weight
to compensate for the under-represented severe and critical grades and
simultaneously penalizes the misclassification of the severe and critical
images that are classified as milder grades.

or determined workers' income directly (``lucky outcomes''). We find that
participants redistribute less and are less reactive to changes in the

implications for models that seek to understand and predict redistribution
attitudes, and help to explain the gap between lab evidence on support for
redistribution and U.S. inequality trends.

consistently distinguish between luck that magnifies effort and luck that
determines income. We also find that participants with more generous baseline
redistribution attitudes are more likely to distinguish between these two
conceptualizations of luck, which suggests that heterogeneity in attitudes
may be partly driven by differences in moral hazard reasoning ability.
Finally, we find that participants with more experience in the workforce
distinction between lucky opportunities and lucky outcomes, but are no different
in lab settings. Our findings suggest that the conceptual framework used by
laypeople has the potential to be improved through work experience.
  Last, we examine how these concepts are related to three other concepts that
are prevalent in the lay literature, (1) merit, (2) skill, and (3) luck in
ability. We find that these concepts are distinct and are influenced by
changes in the importance of luck in determining opportunities and outcomes.
For example, if luck in ability increases, participants reduce their
redistribution and award lower wages to workers with low ability. We also find
that if luck in skill increases, participants become less reactive to
changes in the average skill of workers they are asked to redistribute for.
Finally, we find that luck in merit influences attitudes towards
redistribution, but only in environments with lucky opportunities.
  Overall, our findings have implications for models that seek to understand
and predict redistribution attitudes and behavior, and help to explain the gap
between lab evidence on support for redistribution and U.S. inequality trends.

be higher than the original gradient norm for some data points, which

affects ML models with different overcomplete parameterizations (e.g.,

understanding the effect of data quality to ML training and offers a means to
definitively identify the data points with the most gain from recurement.

) aims to learn effective
multi-agent policies from pre-collected datasets, which is an important step
toward the deployment of multi-agent systems in real-world applications.
However, in practice, each individual behavior policy that generates
multi-agent joint trajectories usually has a different level of how well it
performs. e.g., an agent is a random policy while other agents are medium
policies. In the cooperative game with global reward, one agent learned by
existing offline MARL often inherits this random policy, jeopardizing the
performance of the entire team. In this paper, we investigate offline MARL with
explicit consideration on the diversity of agent-wise trajectories and propose
a novel framework called Shared Individual Trajectories (SIT) to address this
problem. Specifically, an attention-based reward decomposition network assigns
the credit to each agent through a differentiable key-value memory mechanism in
an offline manner. These decomposed credits are then used to reconstruct the
joint offline datasets into prioritized experience replay with individual
trajectories, afterwards agents can be trained jointly. We evaluate our method
on both discrete and continuous multi-agent benchmarks with various levels of
trajectories, and the results show our approach is superior to existing
methods.

same properties as the Raman transitions used for the M{\o}lmer-S{\o}rensen
gate, up to a unitary transformation.

of human beings. Scientific
literature, as the major medium that carries knowledge, plays a significant
role in knowledge transmission, scientific progress, and academic development.
However, there are still many challenges in knowledge transmission due to the
rapid growth of the scale of scientific literature and the increasing diversity
of document formats. At present, many scholars tend to rely on search
engines to quickly find the information they need, but there are still many
insufficient problems, such as information overload, and low search efficiency.
To this end, we advocate the use of graph neural networks (GNNs) based on the
knowledge graph (KG) to search for scientific information and propose a novel
academic search system named AcademicNeT based on GNNs. This system aggregates
scientists, papers, and institutions into a unified knowledge graph and uses a
variety of GNN models to search for information. Our system outperforms the
common search engines in terms of search accuracy and efficiency. The code and
data are available at https://github.com/huanyong2017/ AcademicNeT.

optimization techniques to find the power loading at the source and relay

allocation at all transmitting nodes for the fixed subcarrier allocation and

sembles of coupled oscillators map
to different functional states in a wide range of applications, e.g., active
and resting states in the brain and stable and unstable power grid
configurations. For this reason, explosive synchronization transitions, which
facilitate fast, abrupt changes between these functional states, has recently
seen significant interest from researchers. While previous work has identified
properties of complex systems that support explosive synchronization, these
investigations have been conducted largely on an ad-hoc basis. Here we provide
an exact criterion for explosive synchronization in coupled phase oscillator
ensembles by investigating the necessary relationship between dynamical and
structural disorder. This result provides a critical step towards untangling
the intertwined properties of complex systems responsible for abrupt phase
transitions and bistability in biological and engineered systems.
Specifically, our analysis reveals that the location of the explosive
transition depends solely on the average dynamical disorder, while the height of
the transition (i.e., its abruptness) is controlled by the variance of the
disorder. These findings hold true for a wide range of coupling functions and
ensemble sizes. Moreover, we show that both ordered and disordered systems
exhibit bistability in the presence of time-invariant noise, which may be of
particular interest for biological and biomedical applications.
Finally, we verify our exact results numerically and derive approximate analytic
expressions that provide insight into the underlying dynamics of the system.
Overall, this work provides a fundamental understanding of the necessary
relationship between disorder and abrupt synchronization transitions in
coupled-oscillator systems.

magnetization vanishes, but its values depend on the concentration~$p$.
Simulations on a random graph also show that a small concentration of Ising
agents is sufficient to induce a ferromagnetic ordering.
  We explain the compatibility of Ising and voter agents by a following simple
argument. Two voters never change their opinions, that are the same as in the
Ising model. Thus, the effect of voters is to increase the concentration of the
preferred state in the Ising system.
  Numerical simulations for the system on a tree show that the model has a
majority voting rule, characteristic for the voter model. An interesting
feature appears when the tree expands to the Bethe lattice. The concentrations
of Ising and voter agents, as well as the opinion (state) are important
parameters that determine whether in the system a long range order or a
chaotic behavior appears.
  For a constant concentration of Ising agents, numerical results show that for
a low concentration the system has a a majority voting rule, but for a high
concentration it is an Ising system. An interesting feature appears when the
concentration of Ising agents depends on the degree $k$ of the node: in that
case, even a small concentration is sufficient to induce a long range order.
An important feature of the opinion formation is the majority voting rule,
which is equivalent to a single voter model. If in the system there is already
a majority of agents with a certain opinion, an addition of another voter

of rat. Their peculiar firing patterns, which correlate with periodic locations
in the environment, led to early hypothesis that grid cells may provide some
form of metric for space. Subsequent research has since uncovered a wealth of
new insights into the characteristics of grid cells and their neural
neighborhoods, the so-called grid cell networks. This review aims to provide a
comprehensive summary of the current grid cell literature in light of a
search for a spatial metric. We argue that any such metric must allow for the
efficient determination of distances and directions between any two locations.
While early grid cell studies have demonstrated a periodic correlation with
location, these studies did not fully characterize the performance of grid
cells in this regard. Here, we evaluate the performance of grid cells from the
perspective of a potential spatial metric. We show that single grid cells
provide only a coarse metric, while the combined signal of a full grid cell
network allows for the determination of distances with a precision of about
25cm and directional information with an accuracy of about 45 degrees. This
performance is significantly better than that of many other animal species,
which rely on visual cues for their metric. Interestingly, the precision of the
grid cell metric is independent of the level of visual acuity of the animal.
Moreover, the grid cell metric is found to be internal with respect to the
animal's environment, in so far as it is not based on any external reference
system. Finally, we show that the firing fields of place cells can be
reconstructed from the grid cell metric. In conclusion, the grid cell metric
deserves a place alongside other celebrated animal metrics, such as the
magnetic field metric of magnetotactic fish and birds, the visual metric of
many insect species and the sound metric of bats and whales.

evolution of Venus's atmosphere is controlled by the planet's primordial
differentiation, which delivered heat and chemicals to the mantle and crust,
which in turn regulate the geochemical and geological activity. The existence
of volcanism throughout the history of Venus suggests a relatively young planet
with continuous magmatic activity, possibly fueled by mantle heat sources.
Partial melting of the subducted crust and the planeticule hypothesis are two
possibilities that could supply water to the upper atmosphere of Venus. The
existence of water in the form of oxides or ice in the deep interior of Venus,
and the role of core-mantle exchange in modulating its atmosphere, are
hypothetical but intriguing possibilities that deserve further exploration.

atmospheric change. The atmospheric change on a global scale is also induced by
small-scale events, such as lightning, electrical discharges in clouds, and
volcanic explosions. Electrical discharges in clouds can induce chemical
reactions that modulate the atmospheric composition both locally and globally.

cycling of Venus's atmosphere highlights the complexity of the planet's system
and the need for multi-disciplinary studies.

## Step 1: Definition of partial uniform ellipticity for level sets
The level sets of a function $f : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}$ are the sets of the
form $S_c = \{ x \in \mathbb{R}^n : f(x) = c \}$, with $c \in \mathbb{R}$. If $f$
is symmetric concave, then its level sets are convex and symmetric with
respect to the origin. The partial uniform ellipticity for level sets is the
following property: there exists $\varepsilon > 0$ such that for every $c \in
\mathbb{R}$ and every $x, y \in S_c$ with $|x - y| \leq \varepsilon |x|$, one has
$|x| \leq C |y|$, for some $C \geq 1$.
## Step 2: Discussion of the definition
This property is a generalization of the classical definition of uniform
ellipticity which refers to the matrix $D^2 f(x)$, with $x$ fixed. Here, we
consider the matrix $D^2 f(x)$ with $x$ varying along the level sets of $f$.
## Step 3: Relation with the Hessian matrix
If $f$ is twice differentiable, then $D^2 f(x)$ is a symmetric matrix. If
f is not twice differentiable, then $D^2 f(x)$ may be a non-symmetric matrix,
but the definition of partial uniform ellipticity for level sets still holds.

for autonomous mobile platforms. Especially when conditions worsen, typical
sensor modalities may fail to operate optimally and subsequently provide inapt
input for safe navigation control. In this study, we present an approach for
the navigation of a dynamic indoor environment with a mobile platform with a
single (and possibly failing) odometry sensor. The proposed framework uses a
combined state estimation strategy that leverages the advantages of
fusion-based estimation and relevantization. While the latter is typically
applied in scenarios with multiple robots, our work shows that it is also
applicable to the single robot case. This results in optimal performance in
varied indoor environments and allows for relevant state estimation when a
single sensor is failing. Both simulation and real-world experiments are
presented, including outdoor experiments in rain conditions.
  We show that the proposed approach outperforms both single-sensor estimation
and cooperative fusion approaches. Furthermore, we present a new open-source
framework for state estimation and control that enables to easily switch and
combine estimation strategies. This framework is available online at
https://github.com/ISDA-UM/RelevanceFramework.
  Navigation in varied and dynamic indoor environments remains a complex task
for autonomous mobile platforms. Especially when conditions worsen, typical
sensor modalities may fail to operate optimally and subsequently provide inapt
input for safe navigation control. In this study, we present an approach for
the navigation of a dynamic environment with a mobile platform with a single
odometry sensor.
  The proposed framework uses a combined state estimation strategy that leverages
state estimation from absolute and relative odometry measurements. While this
approach was previously proposed in Sahbani et al., we extend this work by
dynamically adapting the weight of the relative odometry measurements based on
new measurements from an available compass. In addition, we present an
efficient filter architecture that separates the fast (providing invariance to
high-frequency noise) and globally-convergent iterations. Both simulation and
real-world experiments are presented, including outdoor experiments in rain
conditions.
  Our experiments show that the proposed approach outperforms single-sensor
estimation approaches and achieves similar performance as cooperative fusion
approaches, while not requiring communication.
  Navigation in varied and dynamic indoor environments remains a complex task
for autonomous mobile platforms. Especially when conditions worsen, typical
sensor modalities may fail to operate optimally and subsequently provide inapt
input for safe navigation control.

Variables (CV), known as asynchronous
polars, are still relatively poorly understood. An asynchronous polar is a
polar in which the spin period of the white dwarf is either shorter or longer
than the binary orbital period (typically within a few percent). The
asynchronous polars have been disproportionately detected in soft gamma-ray
observations, leading us to consider the possibility that they have
intrinsically harder X-ray spectra. We compared standard and asynchronous
polars in order to examine the relationship between a CV's synchronization
status and its spectral shape. Using the entire sample of asynchronous polars,
we find that the asynchronous polars may, indeed, have harder spectra, but that
the result is not statistically significant.
  We also find that the spectral difference is primarily driven by a single
outlier in the asynchronous sample, IP3.
  By examining the published spectral data in more detail, we find that IP3's
spectrum is not representative of the asynchronous polars as a whole.
Removing IP3 from the sample makes it clear that there is no difference in
spectral shape between the asynchronous and synchronous polars.
  Finally, we note that the spectral difference claimed for the asynchronous
polar IP3 has been used to derive a mass for the white dwarf; if this result is
not reliable, then this mass estimate is likely inaccurate.
  We rederive the mass using the latest spectral models and consider other
methods of estimating the mass for additional robustness.
We find a mass estimate of $0.85\pm0.03 M_\odot$ using the spectral fit,
consistent with other methods which give $M_\text{WD} \approx 0.8 M_\odot$.
The new spectral fit and derived mass estimate highlight the importance of
including systematic uncertainties when using techniques for estimating the
properties of CV components.
Finally, we stress that even if the asynchronous polars do have harder spectra,
the effect is not large enough to be of interest for any but the best
observed objects.
  Based on the final result, we do not recommend further investigation of this
question.

a core theory for dependently typed
programming and higher-order constructive logic. Originally introduced in
Coquand's 1985 thesis, CC has inspired 25 years of research in programming
languages and type theory. Today, extensions of CC form the basis of languages
like Coq and Agda. This survey reviews three proofs of CC's strong
normalization property (the fact that there are no infinite reduction sequences
from well-typed expressions). It highlights the similarities in the structure
of the proofs while showing how their differences are motivated by the varying
goals of their authors.
  We demonstrate this by discussing the proofs in the following order: Tait's
approach for CC, which is an extension of his proof for the simply typed
$\lambda$-calculus; long normal forms, which was originally proved by
Geuens and Levy, but was first published by Huet; and the syntactic closure
property, which was first proved by Cannone and Merlè.
  By comparing the proofs for CC with those for simpler types, we illustrate
the key features of each normalization proof. By comparing the proofs for CC
itself, we show how different goals lead to different approaches to the same
problem.
  Finally, we discuss the lessons that can be learned from these comparisons,
highlighting the importance of a clear formulation of the problem to be
solved, and how different problems might require different solutions. We
conclude by outlining some directions for future work on normalization proofs.
  We hope that this survey illustrates the beauty and importance of
normalization proofs, making it accessible to a wider audience and showing how
their differences are motivated by varying goals.

architectures, and especially the increasing number of mispredicted branches,

hotspots, a major cause of mispredicted branches, by dualizing methods into

using qudits over qubits for
scalar Quantum Electrodynamics in $(1+1)$d. We measure the mass gap using an
out of time correlator as a function of noise coming from an amplitude damping
error channel and a generalized Pauli channel decoherence channel for both
qubits and qutrits. For the same error in determination of the mass, the qutrit
simulations can tolerate 10 to 100x larger gate noise than a qubit simulations.

future with a qutrits but is infeasible using qubits.

the simulation. We define a window around the mass gap and measure the number of
non-zero states within that window as a function of lattice size and qutrit
occupation number. We find that the number of effective degrees of freedom
scales as the square root of qutrit occupation number for both qutrit and qubit
simulations.

We define a new measure of entanglement that is independent of the choice of
basis and use it to compare qutrit and qubit two and three body entanglement. We
find that qutrits can exhibit non-abundant entanglement in a three-body state,
which is not possible with qubits.

quantum simulations of interacting theories.

worth the expense and should be a priority for quantum computing resources.
Finally, we show that even with current level of qutrit availability, we can
obtain meaningful results for simulating interacting theories.

OS temperature sensor for
densely-distributed thermal monitoring in systems on chip. The sensor front
end is based on a sub-threshold MOSFET bridge whose resistive elements are
implemented as long channel (80$\mu$m) MOSFETs. Due to the long channel
characteristics, the bridge has a clear DC output as soon as the supply
voltage overcomes the absolute temperature, thus allowing the temperature
measurement in a very wide range (from 0K to a fraction of the absolute
temperature). The sensor back end is based on a low-power SAR ADC with 10 bits
of resolution that achieves a measure rate of 1.68kHz. The whole sensor
occupies an area of 0.021$mm^2$ and it is designed in a 180nm CMOS technology.
The peak of energy consumption occurs at 25C with a value of 1.24$\mu$W. This
work presents a novel MOSFET bridge for temperature measurement with clear DC
output and it is suitable for several system-on-chip applications.
Moreover, the use of sub-threshold MOSFETs reduces the consumption with respect
to junction temperature sensors. The measurement accuracy is -1.35C for 3\sigma
and it is obtained by properly sizing the MOSFETs that compose the bridge. The
proposed sensor achieves an excellent figure-of-merit of 0.065pJ/^\circ C.
  As this work is a sensor presentation, a thermal sensor system is not
assembled around the sensor. However, to fully evaluate the sensor performance
a realistic thermal stress is applied to the die by using a hot chip technique.
In this scenario, the sensor is able to measure a temperature gradient.
Moreover, to evaluate the sensor accuracy, a calibration procedure is presented
and it is based on a least square method. The presented sensor is a sensible
tool to evaluate the thermal behavior of SOCs, to optimize the thermal
designs and to implement distributed thermal monitoring systems.

state of the art; Section II explains the proposed sensor architecture;

G) approach is a powerful tool for
studies of a large variety of systems, ranging from statistical physics over
the theory of the strong interaction to gravity. The practical application of
this approach relies on the derivation of so-called flow equations, which
describe the change of the quantum effective action under the variation of a
coarse-graining parameter. In the present work, we discuss in detail a novel
approach to solve such flow equations. This approach relies on the fact that RG
equations can be rewritten such that they exhibit similarities with the
conservation laws of fluid dynamics. This observation can be exploited in
different ways. First of all, we show that this allows to employ powerful
numerical techniques developed in the context of fluid dynamics to solve RG
equations. In particular, it allows us to reliably treat the emergence of
nonanalytic behavior in the RG flow of the effective action as it is expected
to occur in studies of, e.g., spontaneous symmetry breaking. Second, the
analogy between RG equations and fluid dynamics offers the opportunity to gain
novel insights into RG flows and their interpretation in general. This includes
the observation that RG flows can be studied as the flow of an fluid phase
space, where the topology of this space is determined by the symmetry breaking
pattern of the system under investigation. As a consequence, many RG flows
will be terminated in fixed points and their qualitative properties can be
studied without solving the RG equations directly. Instead, the behavior of the
systems under investigation is determined by the topology of the flow as
determined by the fixed points and the topology of the original parameter space.

music, people still rely on textual search engines like Google. We propose Pied
piper, a meta search engine for music. It can search for music lyrics, song
metadata and song audio or a combination of any of these as the input query and
efficiently return the relevant results.
  The system architecture is designed with search as the core functionality.
It has three main components - index component, search component and result
renderer component. The index component indexes the data from multiple sources.
These indexes are then used by the search component to perform efficient
queries. The result renderer component renders the search results to the user.
It contains a user interface where the user can input a query and see the
search results.
  We have indexed data from two sources - Lifehacks (a song metadata
database) and lyricwiki (lyric database for many songs). Lifehacks has around
1.5 million song entries and around 10,000 artists entries. Lyricwiki has
around 1.5 million song entries and around 20,000 artist entries. The indexing
is done using LevelDB, a key value store. The search component uses a
bidimensional index to perform efficient queries. The results are then rendered
to the user using a simple UI written in Python's Tkinter library and JavaScript
in jQuery.
  We have performed around 120,000 searches and see constant search performance
of around 0.5s per search, independent of the number of indexes and the data
volume being searched.
  The system is designed with extensibility in mind. It can be extended to
include search for audio by integrating an audio search engine like SoundPrint
or YMusic or by using a generic similarity search engine like ANNOY.
  The system can also be made more accurate by incorporating more data sources
and incorporating data integration techniques to combine data from all the
sources. For example, we can index song audio from a music search engine like
SoundPrint or YMusic or generally use a similarity search engine like ANNOY.
Besides accuracy, the system can also be made more user friendly by adding a
more sophisticated UI and a mobile app.
  In summary, this is a well-designed, efficient and extendible system for
internet music search. It has search performance of around 0.5s per search and
can be extended to search for audio by integrating an audio search engine or by
using a generic similarity search engine.

continuum cores in the Dragon infrared dark cloud (also
known as G28.37+0.07 or G28.34+0.06) is analyzed statistically. Based on their
association with molecular outflows, the sample is divided into protostellar
and starless cores. Statistical tests suggest that the protostellar cores are
more massive than the starless cores, even after temperature and opacity biases
are accounted for. We suggest that the mass difference indicates core mass
growth since their formation. The mass growth implies that massive star
formation may not have to start with massive prestellar cores, depending on the
core mass growth rate. Its impact on the relation between core mass function
and stellar initial mass function is to be further explored.
  The mass growth may facilitate the core-wide collapse that can trigger
cluster-mode star formation. If most of the protostellar cores are capable of
forming cluster members, the cluster mass function may extend down to at least
0.8% of solar mass.
  Finally, we discuss how the core mass growth may affect the surrounding
molecular cloud. If the growth rate is approximately 10^-8 M_{\odot} yr^{-1},
and is sustained for about 10 Myr, the total mass in a giant molecular cloud
can be approximately 10^5 M_{\odot}. This may be sufficient to trigger the
global collapse of the cloud, and eventually, a giant star formation event.
The core mass growth may be an important ingredient in the interplay between
star formation and its parent molecular cloud.
  We recommend follow-up observations to further explore the core mass growth,
and to consider the role of this process in massive star and star cluster
formation.
  Finally, we point out that the core mass growth may provide a natural
explanation for the presence of young massive clusters in the galaxy, as the
time scale for cluster formation is shorter than previously assumed.

-high-energy cosmic rays (UHECRs) has
been an unsolved question of high-energy astrophysics. One approach for solving
this puzzle is to correlate UHECRs with high-energy neutrinos, since neutrinos
are a direct probe of hadronic interactions of cosmic rays and are not
deflected by magnetic fields. Here we report on the search for correlations
between the Pierre Auger Observatory UHECR data and neutrino data from the
IceCube and ANTARES collaborations using a maximum likelihood method. No
significant correlation is found when comparing the arrival directions of UHECRs
with neutrino data in the neutrino energy range from a few TeV to a few EeV.
Using neutrino data from the IceCube collaboration, we derive upper limits on the
correlation probability for UHECRs and neutrinos of $\sim 2 \cdot 10^{-3}
\,\mathrm{sr}^{-1}\,\mathrm{yr}^{-1}$ for $E_\mathrm{CR} \geq 57\,\mathrm{EeV}$
and $\sim 3 \cdot 10^{-2} \,\mathrm{sr}^{-1}\,\mathrm{yr}^{-1}$ for
$E_\mathrm{CR} \geq 40\,\mathrm{EeV}$, depending on the neutrino energy. These
results do not favor a hadronic primary composition and hadronic interaction
mechanisms for UHECRs at energies above $\sim 40\,\mathrm{EeV}$.
  Finally, we derive a limit on the fraction of neutrino flux produced by UHECRs
via photoproduction of neutrinos, $f_\mathrm{\nu UHECR} < 0.13\%$ for
$E_\mathrm{\nu} \geq 400\,\mathrm{GeV}$, which will become relevant for future
neutrino detectors.
  The search for correlations between UHECR and neutrino data is an ongoing
effort and the final answer will be provided by future detectors with higher
sensitivity, such as the planned AMIGA muon detector at the Pierre Auger
Observatory or the effective neutrino detection volume of a next-generation
under-ice neutrino telescope in Antarctica.

effort. Globus, an early and influential grid computing project, faced
technical, social, and political challenges in its development and deployment.

to overcome these challenges and achieve widespread adoption. We find that this
success can be partially attributed to a translational approach, in which the

carefully crafted architecture that reflected a translational design, and how
this architecture facilitated the development of a national grid infrastructure
with billions of dollars of funding. Finally, we reflect on how a translational
framing can be used to develop computing systems that are designed to
effectively address large-scale application needs, and why it is important to
do so in order to realize the full potential of our computational investments.

  This article describes our type-based static verification tool HELMHOLTZ for
Michelson, which is a statically typed stack-based language for writing smart
contracts that are executed on the blockchain platform Tezos. HELMHOLTZ is
designed on top of our extension of Michelson's type system with refinement
types. HELMHOLTZ takes a Michelson program annotated with a user-defined
specification written in the form of a refinement type as input; it then
typechecks the program against the specification based on the refinement type
system, discharging the generated verification conditions with the SMT solver
Z3. We briefly introduce our refinement type system for the core calculus
Mini-Michelson of Michelson, which incorporates the characteristic features
such as compound datatypes (e.g., lists and pairs), higher-order functions, and
invocation of another contract. \HELMHOLTZ{} successfully verifies several
practical Michelson programs, including one that transfers money to an account
and that checks a digital signature.

natural deduction. Therefore, the merit over pseudocode is that each statement

approach for solving a problem. As demonstrated in the sorting problem, the

imperative way first. The structure of the logical pseudocode of sorting is

variables $U_1,\dots, U_n$ with $P(U_i=U_j)=0$ for $i\not=j$ and

result shows that strictly cyclic $n$-tuples are ubiquitous: any $n$ with an
element in $\{2,3,4,5,6,10\}$ is the first coordinate of a strictly cyclic

under a weaker assumption of independence: if $U_1,\dots,U_n$ are exchangeable
random variables with $P(U_1=1)=\dots=P(U_n=1)=1$ and $P(U_1<\dots<U_n)>0$,

variables with $P(U_i=1)$ constant for $i=1,\dots,14$, then

propose a novel cycleGAN architecture using a single switchable generator. The
core idea is that we enforce the cycle-consistency by switching the generator
between two distinct translation directions, instead of using the two separate
generators. The advantage of the proposed approach is that only one generator
needs to be trained, which reduces the memory requirement and the number of
learnable parameters. Thanks to these advantages, the cycleGAN training is
considerably easier and more stable. The effectiveness of the proposed method

denoising and cross-domain medical image translation. Experimental results
